The author of al-Tahrir said: The strength of the speech indicates that the meaning of "you give thanks" is "you believe," until it stands opposite to disbelief; and God Exalted has named righteous deeds and acts of obedience "thanks" in His saying: ﴿Work, family of Dawud, in thanks﴾ [Saba': 13]. End of quotation.

The discussion of this verse has already preceded in Saba'.

Al-Nahwiyyan (the two grammarians, Abu Amr and al-Kisa'i) and Ibn Kathir read ﴿yardahu﴾ by connecting the damma of the ha' to a waw; Ibn Amir and Hafs read with a damma only; Abu Bakr read with a sukun on the ha'. Abu Hatim said: this is an error and not permissible. End of quotation.

It is not an error; rather, that is a dialect of the Banu Kilab and Banu ʿUqayl. As for His saying: "and no bearer bears the burden of another" up to "the contents of the breasts," its discussion has already preceded.

This surah is Meccan. Ibn 'Abbas reported an exception: ﴿Allah has sent down the best of speech﴾ [al-Zumar: 23] and ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed﴾ [al-Zumar: 53]. Muqatil reported an exception: ﴿O My servants who have transgressed﴾ [al-Zumar: 53], and His saying: ﴿Say: O My servants who believe, fear your Lord. For those who do good in this world there is good﴾ [al-Zumar: 10]. Some of the early scholars (al-salaf) reported an exception: ﴿O My servants who have transgressed﴾ [al-Zumar: 53] up to His saying "they perceive" (taz'urun), three verses. Some of them reported that the exception is seven verses, from His saying: ﴿O My servants who have transgressed﴾ [al-Zumar: 53].

Its connection with the end of the preceding surah is that the previous surah ended with His saying: "It is nothing but a reminder to the worlds," and this surah begins: "The revelation of the Book from Allah, the Mighty, the Wise."

Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: "Tanzil" (revelation) is the subject (mubtada'), and "from Allah" is the predicate (khabar), or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "This is tanzil." "From Allah" is connected to "tanzil." I say: it is the predicate, and the subject is "huwa" (it), referring back to His saying: "It is nothing but a reminder to the worlds." As if it were said: "And what is this reminder?" Then it was said: "It is the revelation of the Book."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Or it is not a complement (silah), meaning 'from Allah,' like your saying: 'This book is from so-and-so to so-and-so.' On this view it is a predicate after a predicate, or the predicate of an omitted subject whose estimate is: 'This is the revelation of the Book; this is from Allah.' Or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) of 'tanzil,' in which the meaning of indication (ishara) operates." End of quotation.

It is not permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause in which the meaning of indication operates, because the meanings of verbs do not operate when what they govern is omitted. For this reason they refuted Abu al-'Abbas (al-Mubarrad) regarding his statement on the verse of al-Farazdaq:

"And when they are not like them in humanity (bashar)."

They said that "mithlahum" (like them) is in the accusative by an omitted predicate, which is estimated: "And that what exists is, in the state of their likeness, a human (bashar)."

It appears that "the Book" is the Qur'an. It is repeated in His saying: "Indeed We sent it down to you, the Book," for the sake of magnification and exaltation. Its being in a clause other than the preceding one takes into account its attribution to the pronoun of majesty, the honouring of the one to whom it was sent down by address, and its specification by "bil-haqq" (with truth). Ibn Abi 'Ablah, Zayd ibn 'Ali and 'Isa read "tanzila" in the accusative, meaning: "Recite and persist."

Ibn 'Atiyya said: The exegetes said regarding "tanzil al-Kitab" that it is the Qur'an. It appears to me that it is a general term for all the books that were sent down from Allah, and it is as if He informed, in a simple report, that the guiding and legislating books, their revelation is only from Allah. He made this report a preface and an introduction to His saying: "Indeed We sent it down to you, the Book." "The Mighty" refers to His power, and "the Wise" to His originating. The second "Book" is the Qur'an, and it admits of nothing other than that.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say: what is meant by 'the Book'? I say: On the first aspect, the apparent meaning is that it is the Qur'an, and on the second that it is the surah." End of quotation.

"Bil-haqq" (with truth) is in the position of a circumstantial clause, meaning: "accompanied by truth," and it is the firm truthfulness in what We deposited in it regarding the affirmation of monotheism (tawhid), prophethood, the return (ma'ad), and the obligations. All of this is truth and sincerity that must be believed in and acted upon. Or "bil-haqq" means: with the proof that it is from Allah, which is the inability of the eloquent to produce its like.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: that is, containing the truth in it, in its rulings and in its reports. Or it means entitlement (istihqaq), and the inclusion of benefit for the world in their guidance and their calling to Allah. End of summary.

When He, the Exalted, bestowed favour upon His Messenger by sending down the Book to him with truth, and the truth was the sincerity of worship to Allah, He commanded him to worship Him, saying: ﴿So worship Allah﴾. As if this command arises from the sending down of the Book, the "fa" (so) in it is for connection, as you say: "Zayd did good to you, so thank him."

"Mukhlisan" (sincerely) means: purifying, "lahu al-din" (for Him the religion): from polytheism, ostentation, and everything else that corrupts it.

The majority read "al-din" in the accusative. Ibn Abi 'Ablah read it in the nominative as the subject (fa'il) of "mukhlisan," and the returning pronoun to the one in the state (dhu al-hal) is omitted according to the opinion of the Basrans, meaning: "the religion is from you." Or "al" is a substitute for the pronoun, meaning: "your religion."

Al-Zamakhshari said: The right of one who reads it in the nominative is to read "mukhlasan" with a fatha on the lam, as in His saying: ﴿And they sincerely devoted their religion to Allah﴾ [al-Nisa': 146], so that it corresponds to His saying: ﴿Surely, to Allah belongs the pure religion﴾. "Al-khalis" and "al-mukhlas" are one, except that he describes the religion with the attribute of its owner by way of metaphorical attribution, like their saying: "the poetry of a poet." End of quotation.

As for one who makes "mukhlisan" a circumstantial clause of the worshipper, and "lahu al-din" a subject and predicate, he has produced an i'rab by which the speech returns to your saying: "To Allah belongs the religion," meaning: "To Allah belongs the pure religion." End of quotation.

We have already mentioned its derivation as the subject of "mukhlisan," and we estimated what links the circumstantial clause to its referent. Among those who held that "lahu al-din" is a new sentence, a subject and predicate, is al-Farra'.

﴿Surely, to Allah belongs the pure religion﴾: that is, free from every taint and turbidity. He is the one to whom obedience must be made sincere, because of His knowledge of the unseen and the secrets, and because His favour upon His servants is pure, without seeking any benefit from them.

Al-Hasan said: "The pure religion" is Islam. Qatada said: it is the testimony that there is no god but Allah.

"Wa-alladhina attakhadhu" (and those who took): is the subject (mubtada'). The apparent meaning is that they are the polytheists. It is possible that the predicate is an omitted "qala" (they said), whose reported speech is His saying: ﴿We do not worship them﴾, meaning: and the polytheists who took besides Allah protectors said: "We do not worship those protectors except that they may bring us near to Allah in nearness (zulfa)." It is also possible that the predicate is: ﴿Indeed Allah will judge between them﴾, and that omitted saying is in the position of a circumstantial clause, meaning: they took them, saying "We do not worship them." Al-Zamakhshari permitted that the predicate be "Indeed Allah will judge," and that the omitted "qalu" (they said) be a substitute for "attakhadhu" (they took), the relative clause of "alladhina," so it has no position in the i'rab, and it is as if it were a substitute of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal).

In the codex of 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud): "They said: we do not worship them," and with it he recited, and Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that "wa-alladhina attakhadhu" be in the sense of "those who are taken," and they are the angels, 'Isa, al-Lat, al-'Uzza and the like. The pronoun in "attakhadhu" returns to the relative pronoun, which is omitted, and its estimate is: "And those whom the polytheists took as protectors," and "awliya'" (protectors) is the second object. This which he permitted is contrary to the apparent meaning, and this saying is widespread among the Arabs. Some of them said this about the angels, and some about the idols and images.

Mujahid said: Some Jews said this about 'Uzayr, and some Christians about the Messiah. It was read: "ma na'buduhum" with a damma on the nun, following the vowel of the ba'.

﴿Indeed Allah will judge between them﴾: He restricted His response to mere threat. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in "baynahum" (between them) returns to those who took and those who were taken. The judgment between them is by admitting the angels and 'Isa, peace be upon him, into Paradise, and by casting into the Fire those who worshipped them along with the stones and wood that they carved and worshipped besides Allah, punishing them with them, as He makes them and those things fuel for Hell. Their disagreement is that those whom they worshipped, such as the angels and 'Isa, were disavowing them, cursing them, and affirming the oneness of Allah. It was said: The pronoun in "baynahum" returns to the polytheists and the believers, when they blame them for worshipping idols and they say: ﴿We do not worship them except that they may bring us near to Allah in nearness﴾, and the judgment in that case is on the Day of Resurrection between the two groups.

﴿Indeed Allah does not guide one who is a liar, an ungrateful disbeliever﴾: a liar in his claim that Allah has a partner; ungrateful toward the blessings of Allah, since he put disbelief in the place of thankfulness. The meaning is: He does not guide the one upon whom He sets a seal, by dying in disbelief, so it is general. In particular meaning: how many have been guided who previously had lies and disbelief in them? Ibn 'Atiyya said: He does not guide the liar and the disbeliever in the state of their lying and their disbelief.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The intended meaning of the denial of guidance is the denial of divine grace (lutf), marking them with the sign that there is no grace for them, and that in Allah's knowledge they are among the perishing. End of quotation.

This is on the path of the Mu'tazila (i'tizal), the rationalist school that held Allah's acts must follow what is best for humans. Anas ibn Malik, al-Jahdari, al-Hasan, al-A'raj and Ibn Ya'mur read: "kadhdhab kaffar" (intensive forms). Zayd ibn 'Ali read: "kadhub wa-kafur."

Since among their lies was the claim of some of them that the angels are daughters of Allah, and they worshipped them, He followed this with His saying: ﴿Had Allah wished to take a son﴾, honouring Him and making Him a sort of adoptive lord, since it is impossible that this be true of Him, the Exalted, in the known sense of procreation. ﴿He would have chosen﴾, that is, He would have chosen from His creatures whatever He wished as a son by way of adoption. But He, the Exalted, did not wish that, because of His saying: ﴿It is not befitting for the Merciful to take a son﴾ [Maryam: 92]. This is general in taking offspring and in taking by choosing.

What shows that "taking" means adoption and choosing is His saying: "from what He creates" (mimma yakhluqu), that is, from among those He originated and brought into being. Then the Exalted declared Himself absolutely free of such things, saying: "Glory be to Him," then He described Himself with oneness and with dominance over the whole world.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He means that if He wished to take a son, He would be prevented, and it would not be valid, because it is impossible; it could only happen if He chose some of His creation and singled them out and drew them near, as a man singles out his son and draws him near. He has done that with the angels, and you were tempted by it, and His singling them out deceived you, so you claimed that they are His children, out of ignorance of Him and of the reality that He is unlike the realities of bodies and accidents. As if He said: If He wished to take a son, He would not exceed what He has done by choosing whom He wished from His creation, namely the angels; but because of your ignorance of Him you supposed their choosing to be their taking as children. Then you persisted in your ignorance and foolishness, and made them daughters, and you were liars and disbelievers, exaggerating in fabrication against Allah and His angels. End of quotation.

What the structure of "law" (if) and its response indicates is that the choosing of a son from what He creates would follow upon supposing that He took one, but He did not take one, so He does not choose one. As for what al-Zamakhshari mentioned, his saying: "meaning, if He wished" to the end, and his later saying: "As if He said: If He wished to take a son, He would not exceed what He has done by choosing whom He wished from His creation," it is not understood from His saying: ﴿Had Allah wished to take a son, He would have chosen from what He creates whatever He wished﴾.

When the Exalted declared Himself free and described His essence with unity and dominance, He mentioned what indicates that from the origination of the upper and lower worlds with truth, the wrapping of night over day and day over night, the subjection of the two luminaries (the sun and the moon), and their running in one order, and the consistency of their affair as He willed, until a named term, which is the Day of Resurrection, when the structure of this world is ruined and their running ceases. Or until the time of their setting every day and night, or the time of their conjunctions every month.

Tafsir of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 39, verses 1–7 (part 2 of 2):

Al-takwir (the wrapping, i.e., one of the two is lengthened over the other): it is as if part of the one has been wrapped over the other. Ibn Abbas said: "He makes the night enter upon the day." Al-Dahhak said: "He adds to one of them by subtracting from the other."

Abu Ubaydah said: "He makes this enter upon that." Al-Zamakhshari said: "In it there are several aspects. Among them: the night and the day are alternating; this one goes and the other covers its place. When it covers its place, it is as if it has been clothed in it and wrapped around it, just as clothing is wrapped around the one who wears it. Among them: each of the two conceals the other when it comes upon it, so its concealing of the other is likened to a visible thing wrapped around something, which hides what is beyond the glances of the eyes. Among them: this one revolves over that one in continuous succession, so this is likened to the successive turns of a turban, one upon the trace of another." End of quotation.

﴿Is He not the Mighty, the Forgiving?﴾: al-Aziz is the One who cannot be overcome; al-Ghaffar is the One who forgives those who repent. Or it means al-Halim, the Forbearing who does not hasten; forbearance is called forgiveness metaphorically.

When He mentioned what indicates His oneness and His dominion, He mentioned the human being, who is the one charged with the burdens of obligations. He said that He created us from a single soul, which is Adam, peace be upon him. This is because Hawwa' (Eve), as is related, was created from Adam, so the creation came from a single soul through the mediation of Hawwa'. It was also said: He brought forth the offspring of Adam from his back like particles (al-dharr), and then afterward created Hawwa', so according to this view the creation from Adam was without intermediary. On this statement, "thumma" (then) is for the sequence of time; on the first view, it appears that the creation of Hawwa' was after our creation, which is not so. Therefore "thumma" came to order the reports, as if it were said: "Then there was of His command, before that, that He made from her her spouse." So the ordering is not in the time of the making. It was also said: "thumma" is coordinated with the attribute, which is "wahidah" (single), meaning: from a soul that was singular, i.e., stood alone.

"Thumma ja'ala" (then He made): al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: what is the sense of the words of the Exalted, ﴿Then He made from it its spouse﴾, and what does it give of the meaning of delay? I say: they are two signs from among the signs He enumerated, indicating His oneness and His power. This wonder of being split from the very self of Adam, and His creating Hawwa' from his rib (qusayra), are two matters; however, the one He made a continuous custom, while the other was not established as a custom, and no female other than Hawwa' was created from a man. So it was more fitting for it to be a sign and more striking to the wonder of the listener. He therefore joined it with 'thumma' to the first sign, to indicate its distinction in excellence and merit, and its delay from it in what returns to the increase of its being a sign. So it is a delay in status and rank, not a delay in existence." End of quotation.

As for ﴿Then He made from it its spouse﴾, the discussion of this "making" has already preceded at the beginning of Surah al-Nisa'.

The description of the livestock as "sent down" (inzal) is metaphorical, either because their provisions are described as descending from the sky, since everything that will exist is written in the Preserved Tablet, or because they subsist on plants, and plants arise from rain, and rain descends from the sky; so it is as if He sent them down. This is like the saying of the poet:

"The humps of the camels in its rain-cloud (rabab)"

meaning: in its cloud. Another said:

"The sop has been placed upon the heads of the sticks"

It was also said: He created them in Paradise and then sent them down; according to this, the sending down of their roots is literal.

Al-an'am (livestock): camels, cattle, sheep and goats. "Eight pairs" because each of them is male and female, and a zawj (pair) is what has another of its kind with it; when it stands alone it is a fard (single) and witr (odd). The Exalted said: ﴿So He made from it the two spouses, the male and the female﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 39].

Ibn Zayd said: ﴿creation after creation﴾ means another from the back of Adam and the backs of the fathers. Ikrimah, Mujahid and al-Suddi said: stages, ﴿creation after creation﴾, such as the lump of flesh, the clot and other than these.

Al-Zamakhshari took it up and said: a complete living being after bones clothed with flesh, after bare bones, after the chewed lump, after the clot, after the drop. End of quotation.

Isa and Talhah read ﴿yakhluqukum﴾ with the qaf assimilated into the kaf (idgham).

The three darknesses (al-zulumat al-thalath): the belly, the womb and the amniotic membrane (al-mashimah). It was also said: the loins (al-sulb), the womb and the belly.

﴿That﴾ (dhalikum): a reference to the One characterized by those previously mentioned attributes, from the creation of the heavens and what follows that of acts.

﴿Then how are you turned away?﴾ meaning: how do you turn away from worshipping Him to worshipping other than Him?

﴿If you disbelieve﴾: Ibn Abbas said: it is addressed to the disbelievers whose hearts God did not will to purify. "His servants" are the believers. This is supported by His saying before it: "Then how are you turned away?", and this is for the disbelievers, so "If you disbelieve" came as an address to them. ﴿Indeed God is free of need of you﴾, and of your worship, since no benefit returns to Him from you nor from your worship, for He is the Absolutely Self-Sufficient. Ibn Atiyyah said: it is possible that it addresses all people, because He, exalted is He, is free of need of all of them, while they are needy of Him. End of quotation.

The expression "His servants" is general. It was said: the intended meaning is particular, namely the angels and the believing humans and jinn. "Ridha" (pleasure/approval) here means "irada" (will), so according to this it is an attribute of essence. It was also said: the intended meaning is generality, as the wording indicates, and ridha is different from irada; it is expressed by it to mean gratitude and reward, i.e., He does not approve for them a religion nor reward them with good by it. So ridha according to this is an attribute of act, in the sense of acceptance and reward.

Ibn Atiyyah said: Consider irada, for its reality is only in what has not yet occurred, while ridha's reality is only in what has already occurred; reflect on this in the verses of the Qur'an and you will find it, though the Arabs may use one in place of the other in their poetry by way of metaphor.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Some deviants have strained to attribute to God what He has negated of His essence, namely approval of disbelief for His servants, and said: this is from the general that is intended to be particular, and He did not intend except His servants whom He meant in His saying: "Indeed My servants, you have no authority over them" [al-Hijr: 42], meaning the protected ones, due to His saying: "a spring from which God's servants drink" [al-Insan: 6]. Exalted is God above what the wrongdoers say. End of quotation.

Thus he called ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbbas, the interpreter of the Qur'an, and the leading scholars of the Sunnah, "some deviants," and applied to them the name of wrongdoers, and that is from his foolishness and audacity, as I said in my qasida in which I mentioned what is to be criticized in it:

"He insults the leading imams with misguidance, especially if they have entered him into narrow straits."

﴿And if you give thanks, He is pleased with it for you﴾: Ibn Abbas said: He multiplies it for you, and it seems he means the reward of gratitude; it was also said: He accepts it from you. The author of al-Tahrir said: The strength of the speech indicates that the meaning of "you give thanks" is "you believe," until it stands opposite to disbelief; and God Exalted has named righteous deeds and acts of obedience "thanks" in His saying: ﴿Work, family of Dawud, in thanks﴾ [Saba': 13]. ﴿Surely, to Allah belongs the pure religion﴾: that is, free from every taint and turbidity. He is the one to whom obedience must be made sincere, because of His knowledge of the unseen and the secrets, and because His favour upon His servants is pure, without seeking any benefit from them.

Al-Hasan said: "The pure religion" is Islam. Qatada said: it is the testimony that there is no god but Allah.

"Wa-alladhina attakhadhu" (and those who took): is the subject (mubtada'). The apparent meaning is that they are the polytheists. It is possible that the predicate is an omitted "qala" (they said), whose reported speech is His saying: ﴿We do not worship them﴾, meaning: and the polytheists who took besides Allah protectors said: "We do not worship those protectors except that they may bring us near to Allah in nearness (zulfa)." It is also possible that the predicate is: ﴿Indeed Allah will judge between them﴾, and that omitted saying is in the position of a circumstantial clause, meaning: they took them, saying "We do not worship them." Al-Zamakhshari permitted that the predicate be "Indeed Allah will judge," and that the omitted "qalu" (they said) be a substitute for "attakhadhu" (they took), the relative clause of "alladhina," so it has no position in the i'rab, and it is as if it were a substitute of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal).

In the codex of 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud): "They said: we do not worship them," and with it he recited, and Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that "wa-alladhina attakhadhu" be in the sense of "those who are taken," and they are the angels, 'Isa, al-Lat, al-'Uzza and the like. The pronoun in "attakhadhu" returns to the relative pronoun, which is omitted, and its estimate is: "And those whom the polytheists took as protectors," and "awliya'" (protectors) is the second object. This which he permitted is contrary to the apparent meaning, and this saying is widespread among the Arabs. Some of them said this about the angels, and some about the idols and images.

Mujahid said: Some Jews said this about 'Uzayr, and some Christians about the Messiah. It was read: "ma na'buduhum" with a damma on the nun, following the vowel of the ba'.

﴿Indeed Allah will judge between them﴾: He restricted His response to mere threat. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in "baynahum" (between them) returns to those who took and those who were taken. The judgment between them is by admitting the angels and 'Isa, peace be upon him, into Paradise, and by casting into the Fire those who worshipped them along with the stones and wood that they carved and worshipped besides Allah, punishing them with them, as He makes them and those things fuel for Hell. Their disagreement is that those whom they worshipped, such as the angels and 'Isa, were disavowing them, cursing them, and affirming the oneness of Allah. It was said: The pronoun in "baynahum" returns to the polytheists and the believers, when they blame them for worshipping idols and they say: ﴿We do not worship them except that they may bring us near to Allah in nearness﴾, and the judgment in that case is on the Day of Resurrection between the two groups.

﴿Indeed Allah does not guide one who is a liar, an ungrateful disbeliever﴾: a liar in his claim that Allah has a partner; ungrateful toward the blessings of Allah, since he put disbelief in the place of thankfulness. The meaning is: He does not guide the one upon whom He sets a seal, by dying in disbelief, so it is general. In particular meaning: how many have been guided who previously had lies and disbelief in them? Ibn 'Atiyya said: He does not guide the liar and the disbeliever in the state of their lying and their disbelief.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The intended meaning of the denial of guidance is the denial of divine grace (lutf), marking them with the sign that there is no grace for them, and that in Allah's knowledge they are among the perishing. End of quotation.

This is on the path of the Mu'tazila (i'tizal), the rationalist school that held Allah's acts must follow what is best for humans. Anas ibn Malik, al-Jahdari, al-Hasan, al-A'raj and Ibn Ya'mur read: "kadhdhab kaffar" (intensive forms). Zayd ibn 'Ali read: "kadhub wa-kafur."

Since among their lies was the claim of some of them that the angels are daughters of Allah, and they worshipped them, He followed this with His saying: ﴿Had Allah wished to take a son﴾, honouring Him and making Him a sort of adoptive lord, since it is impossible that this be true of Him, the Exalted, in the known sense of procreation. ﴿He would have chosen﴾, that is, He would have chosen from His creatures whatever He wished as a son by way of adoption. But He, the Exalted, did not wish that, because of His saying: ﴿It is not befitting for the Merciful to take a son﴾ [Maryam: 92]. This is general in taking offspring and in taking by choosing.

What shows that "taking" means adoption and choosing is His saying: "from what He creates" (mimma yakhluqu), that is, from among those He originated and brought into being. Then the Exalted declared Himself absolutely free of such things, saying: "Glory be to Him," then He described Himself with oneness and with dominance over the whole world.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He means that if He wished to take a son, He would be prevented, and it would not be valid, because it is impossible; it could only happen if He chose some of His creation and singled them out and drew them near, as a man singles out his son and draws him near. He has done that with the angels, and you were tempted by it, and His singling them out deceived you, so you claimed that they are His children, out of ignorance of Him and of the reality that He is unlike the realities of bodies and accidents. As if He said: If He wished to take a son, He would not exceed what He has done by choosing whom He wished from His creation, namely the angels; but because of your ignorance of Him you supposed their choosing to be their taking as children. Then you persisted in your ignorance and foolishness, and made them daughters, and you were liars and disbelievers, exaggerating in fabrication against Allah and His angels. End of quotation.

What the structure of "law" (if) and its response indicates is that the choosing of a son from what He creates would follow upon supposing that He took one, but He did not take one, so He does not choose one. As for what al-Zamakhshari mentioned, his saying: "meaning, if He wished" to the end, and his later saying: "As if He said: If He wished to take a son, He would not exceed what He has done by choosing whom He wished from His creation," it is not understood from His saying: ﴿Had Allah wished to take a son, He would have chosen from what He creates whatever He wished﴾.

When the Exalted declared Himself free and described His essence with unity and dominance, He mentioned what indicates that from the origination of the upper and lower worlds with truth, the wrapping of night over day and day over night, the subjection of the two luminaries (the sun and the moon), and their running in one order, and the consistency of their affair as He willed, until a named term, which is the Day of Resurrection, when the structure of this world is ruined and their running ceases. Or until the time of their setting every day and night, or the time of their conjunctions every month.

Tafsir of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 39, verses 1–7 (part 2 of 2):

Al-takwir (the wrapping, i.e., one of the two is lengthened over the other): it is as if part of the one has been wrapped over the other. Ibn Abbas said: "He makes the night enter upon the day." Al-Dahhak said: "He adds to one of them by subtracting from the other."

Abu Ubaydah said: "He makes this enter upon that." Al-Zamakhshari said: "In it there are several aspects. Among them: the night and the day are alternating; this one goes and the other covers its place. When it covers its place, it is as if it has been clothed in it and wrapped around it, just as clothing is wrapped around the one who wears it. Among them: each of the two conceals the other when it comes upon it, so its concealing of the other is likened to a visible thing wrapped around something, which hides what is beyond the glances of the eyes. Among them: this one revolves over that one in continuous succession, so this is likened to the successive turns of a turban, one upon the trace of another." End of quotation.

﴿Is He not the Mighty, the Forgiving?﴾: al-Aziz is the One who cannot be overcome; al-Ghaffar is the One who forgives those who repent. Or it means al-Halim, the Forbearing who does not hasten; forbearance is called forgiveness metaphorically.

When He mentioned what indicates His oneness and His dominion, He mentioned the human being, who is the one charged with the burdens of obligations. He said that He created us from a single soul, which is Adam, peace be upon him. This is because Hawwa' (Eve), as is related, was created from Adam, so the creation came from a single soul through the mediation of Hawwa'. It was also said: He brought forth the offspring of Adam from his back like particles (al-dharr), and then afterward created Hawwa', so according to this view the creation from Adam was without intermediary. On this statement, "thumma" (then) is for the sequence of time; on the first view, it appears that the creation of Hawwa' was after our creation, which is not so. Therefore "thumma" came to order the reports, as if it were said: "Then there was of His command, before that, that He made from her her spouse." So the ordering is not in the time of the making. It was also said: "thumma" is coordinated with the attribute, which is "wahidah" (single), meaning: from a soul that was singular, i.e., stood alone.

"Thumma ja'ala" (then He made): al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: what is the sense of the words of the Exalted, ﴿Then He made from it its spouse﴾, and what does it give of the meaning of delay? I say: they are two signs from among the signs He enumerated, indicating His oneness and His power. This wonder of being split from the very self of Adam, and His creating Hawwa' from his rib (qusayra), are two matters; however, the one He made a continuous custom, while the other was not established as a custom, and no female other than Hawwa' was created from a man. So it was more fitting for it to be a sign and more striking to the wonder of the listener. He therefore joined it with 'thumma' to the first sign, to indicate its distinction in excellence and merit, and its delay from it in what returns to the increase of its being a sign. So it is a delay in status and rank, not a delay in existence." End of quotation.

As for ﴿Then He made from it its spouse﴾, the discussion of this "making" has already preceded at the beginning of Surah al-Nisa'.

The description of the livestock as "sent down" (inzal) is metaphorical, either because their provisions are described as descending from the sky, since everything that will exist is written in the Preserved Tablet, or because they subsist on plants, and plants arise from rain, and rain descends from the sky; so it is as if He sent them down. This is like the saying of the poet:

"The humps of the camels in its rain-cloud (rabab)"

meaning: in its cloud. Another said:

"The sop has been placed upon the heads of the sticks"

It was also said: He created them in Paradise and then sent them down; according to this, the sending down of their roots is literal.

Al-an'am (livestock): camels, cattle, sheep and goats. "Eight pairs" because each of them is male and female, and a zawj (pair) is what has another of its kind with it; when it stands alone it is a fard (single) and witr (odd). The Exalted said: ﴿So He made from it the two spouses, the male and the female﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 39].

Ibn Zayd said: ﴿creation after creation﴾ means another from the back of Adam and the backs of the fathers. Ikrimah, Mujahid and al-Suddi said: stages, ﴿creation after creation﴾, such as the lump of flesh, the clot and other than these.

Al-Zamakhshari took it up and said: a complete living being after bones clothed with flesh, after bare bones, after the chewed lump, after the clot, after the drop. End of quotation.

Isa and Talhah read ﴿yakhluqukum﴾ with the qaf assimilated into the kaf (idgham).

The three darknesses (al-zulumat al-thalath): the belly, the womb and the amniotic membrane (al-mashimah). It was also said: the loins (al-sulb), the womb and the belly.

﴿That﴾ (dhalikum): a reference to the One characterized by those previously mentioned attributes, from the creation of the heavens and what follows that of acts.

﴿Then how are you turned away?﴾ meaning: how do you turn away from worshipping Him to worshipping other than Him?

﴿If you disbelieve﴾: Ibn Abbas said: it is addressed to the disbelievers whose hearts God did not will to purify. "His servants" are the believers. This is supported by His saying before it: "Then how are you turned away?", and this is for the disbelievers, so "If you disbelieve" came as an address to them. ﴿Indeed God is free of need of you﴾, and of your worship, since no benefit returns to Him from you nor from your worship, for He is the Absolutely Self-Sufficient. Ibn Atiyyah said: it is possible that it addresses all people, because He, exalted is He, is free of need of all of them, while they are needy of Him. End of quotation.

The expression "His servants" is general. It was said: the intended meaning is particular, namely the angels and the believing humans and jinn. "Ridha" (pleasure/approval) here means "irada" (will), so according to this it is an attribute of essence. It was also said: the intended meaning is generality, as the wording indicates, and ridha is different from irada; it is expressed by it to mean gratitude and reward, i.e., He does not approve for them a religion nor reward them with good by it. So ridha according to this is an attribute of act, in the sense of acceptance and reward.

Ibn Atiyyah said: Consider irada, for its reality is only in what has not yet occurred, while ridha's reality is only in what has already occurred; reflect on this in the verses of the Qur'an and you will find it, though the Arabs may use one in place of the other in their poetry by way of metaphor.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Some deviants have strained to attribute to God what He has negated of His essence, namely approval of disbelief for His servants, and said: this is from the general that is intended to be particular, and He did not intend except His servants whom He meant in His saying: "Indeed My servants, you have no authority over them" [al-Hijr: 42], meaning the protected ones, due to His saying: "a spring from which God's servants drink" [al-Insan: 6]. Exalted is God above what the wrongdoers say. End of quotation.

Thus he called ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbbas, the interpreter of the Qur'an, and the leading scholars of the Sunnah, "some deviants," and applied to them the name of wrongdoers, and that is from his foolishness and audacity, as I said in my qasida in which I mentioned what is to be criticized in it:

"He insults the leading imams with misguidance, especially if they have entered him into narrow straits."

﴿And if you give thanks, He is pleased with it for you﴾: Ibn Abbas said: He multiplies it for you, and it seems he means the reward of gratitude; it was also said: He accepts it from you. The author of al-Tahrir said: The strength of the speech indicates that the meaning of "you give thanks" is "you believe," until it stands opposite to disbelief; and God Exalted has named righteous deeds and acts of obedience "thanks" in His saying: ﴿Work, family of Dawud, in thanks﴾ [Saba': 13]. End of quotation.

The discussion of this verse has already preceded in Saba'.

Al-Nahwiyyan (the two grammarians, Abu Amr and al-Kisa'i) and Ibn Kathir read ﴿yardahu﴾ by connecting the damma of the ha' to a waw; Ibn Amir and Hafs read with a damma only; Abu Bakr read with a sukun on the ha'. Abu Hatim said: this is an error and not permissible. End of quotation.

It is not an error; rather, that is a dialect of the Banu Kilab and Banu ʿUqayl. As for His saying: "and no bearer bears the burden of another" up to "the contents of the breasts," its discussion has already preceded.

This surah is Meccan. Ibn 'Abbas reported an exception: ﴿Allah has sent down the best of speech﴾ [al-Zumar: 23] and ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed﴾ [al-Zumar: 53]. Muqatil reported an exception: ﴿O My servants who have transgressed﴾ [al-Zumar: 53], and His saying: ﴿Say: O My servants who believe, fear your Lord. For those who do good in this world there is good﴾ [al-Zumar: 10]. Some of the early scholars (al-salaf) reported an exception: ﴿O My servants who have transgressed﴾ [al-Zumar: 53] up to His saying "they perceive" (taz'urun), three verses. Some of them reported that the exception is seven verses, from His saying: ﴿O My servants who have transgressed﴾ [al-Zumar: 53].

Its connection with the end of the preceding surah is that the previous surah ended with His saying: "It is nothing but a reminder to the worlds," and this surah begins: "The revelation of the Book from Allah, the Mighty, the Wise."

Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: "Tanzil" (revelation) is the subject (mubtada'), and "from Allah" is the predicate (khabar), or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "This is tanzil." "From Allah" is connected to "tanzil." I say: it is the predicate, and the subject is "huwa" (it), referring back to His saying: "It is nothing but a reminder to the worlds." As if it were said: "And what is this reminder?" Then it was said: "It is the revelation of the Book."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Or it is not a complement (silah), meaning 'from Allah,' like your saying: 'This book is from so-and-so to so-and-so.' On this view it is a predicate after a predicate, or the predicate of an omitted subject whose estimate is: 'This is the revelation of the Book; this is from Allah.' Or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) of 'tanzil,' in which the meaning of indication (ishara) operates." End of quotation.

It is not permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause in which the meaning of indication operates, because the meanings of verbs do not operate when what they govern is omitted. For this reason they refuted Abu al-'Abbas (al-Mubarrad) regarding his statement on the verse of al-Farazdaq:

"And when they are not like them in humanity (bashar)."

They said that "mithlahum" (like them) is in the accusative by an omitted predicate, which is estimated: "And that what exists is, in the state of their likeness, a human (bashar)."

It appears that "the Book" is the Qur'an. It is repeated in His saying: "Indeed We sent it down to you, the Book," for the sake of magnification and exaltation. Its being in a clause other than the preceding one takes into account its attribution to the pronoun of majesty, the honouring of the one to whom it was sent down by address, and its specification by "bil-haqq" (with truth). Ibn Abi 'Ablah, Zayd ibn 'Ali and 'Isa read "tanzila" in the accusative, meaning: "Recite and persist."

Ibn 'Atiyya said: The exegetes said regarding "tanzil al-Kitab" that it is the Qur'an. It appears to me that it is a general term for all the books that were sent down from Allah, and it is as if He informed, in a simple report, that the guiding and legislating books, their revelation is only from Allah. He made this report a preface and an introduction to His saying: "Indeed We sent it down to you, the Book." "The Mighty" refers to His power, and "the Wise" to His originating. The second "Book" is the Qur'an, and it admits of nothing other than that.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say: what is meant by 'the Book'? I say: On the first aspect, the apparent meaning is that it is the Qur'an, and on the second that it is the surah." End of quotation.

"Bil-haqq" (with truth) is in the position of a circumstantial clause, meaning: "accompanied by truth," and it is the firm truthfulness in what We deposited in it regarding the affirmation of monotheism (tawhid), prophethood, the return (ma'ad), and the obligations. All of this is truth and sincerity that must be believed in and acted upon. Or "bil-haqq" means: with the proof that it is from Allah, which is the inability of the eloquent to produce its like.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: that is, containing the truth in it, in its rulings and in its reports. Or it means entitlement (istihqaq), and the inclusion of benefit for the world in their guidance and their calling to Allah. End of summary.

When He, the Exalted, bestowed favour upon His Messenger by sending down the Book to him with truth, and the truth was the sincerity of worship to Allah, He commanded him to worship Him, saying: ﴿So worship Allah﴾. As if this command arises from the sending down of the Book, the "fa" (so) in it is for connection, as you say: "Zayd did good to you, so thank him."

"Mukhlisan" (sincerely) means: purifying, "lahu al-din" (for Him the religion): from polytheism, ostentation, and everything else that corrupts it.

The majority read "al-din" in the accusative. Ibn Abi 'Ablah read it in the nominative as the subject (fa'il) of "mukhlisan," and the returning pronoun to the one in the state (dhu al-hal) is omitted according to the opinion of the Basrans, meaning: "the religion is from you." Or "al" is a substitute for the pronoun, meaning: "your religion."

Al-Zamakhshari said: The right of one who reads it in the nominative is to read "mukhlasan" with a fatha on the lam, as in His saying: ﴿And they sincerely devoted their religion to Allah﴾ [al-Nisa': 146], so that it corresponds to His saying: ﴿Surely, to Allah belongs the pure religion﴾. "Al-khalis" and "al-mukhlas" are one, except that he describes the religion with the attribute of its owner by way of metaphorical attribution, like their saying: "the poetry of a poet." End of quotation.

As for one who makes "mukhlisan" a circumstantial clause of the worshipper, and "lahu al-din" a subject and predicate, he has produced an i'rab by which the speech returns to your saying: "To Allah belongs the religion," meaning: "To Allah belongs the pure religion." End of quotation.

Or until the time of their setting every day and night, or the time of their conjunctions every month.

Tafsir of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 39, verses 1–7 (part 2 of 2):

Al-takwir (the wrapping, i.e., one of the two is lengthened over the other): it is as if part of the one has been wrapped over the other. Ibn Abbas said: "He makes the night enter upon the day." Al-Dahhak said: "He adds to one of them by subtracting from the other."

Abu Ubaydah said: "He makes this enter upon that." Al-Zamakhshari said: "In it there are several aspects. Among them: the night and the day are alternating; this one goes and the other covers its place. When it covers its place, it is as if it has been clothed in it and wrapped around it, just as clothing is wrapped around the one who wears it. Among them: each of the two conceals the other when it comes upon it, so its concealing of the other is likened to a visible thing wrapped around something, which hides what is beyond the glances of the eyes. Among them: this one revolves over that one in continuous succession, so this is likened to the successive turns of a turban, one upon the trace of another." End of quotation.

﴿Is He not the Mighty, the Forgiving?﴾: al-Aziz is the One who cannot be overcome; al-Ghaffar is the One who forgives those who repent. Or it means al-Halim, the Forbearing who does not hasten; forbearance is called forgiveness metaphorically.

When He mentioned what indicates His oneness and His dominion, He mentioned the human being, who is the one charged with the burdens of obligations. He said that He created us from a single soul, which is Adam, peace be upon him. This is because Hawwa' (Eve), as is related, was created from Adam, so the creation came from a single soul through the mediation of Hawwa'. It was also said: He brought forth the offspring of Adam from his back like particles (al-dharr), and then afterward created Hawwa', so according to this view the creation from Adam was without intermediary. On this statement, "thumma" (then) is for the sequence of time; on the first view, it appears that the creation of Hawwa' was after our creation, which is not so. Therefore "thumma" came to order the reports, as if it were said: "Then there was of His command, before that, that He made from her her spouse." So the ordering is not in the time of the making. It was also said: "thumma" is coordinated with the attribute, which is "wahidah" (single), meaning: from a soul that was singular, i.e., stood alone.

"Thumma ja'ala" (then He made): al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: what is the sense of the words of the Exalted, ﴿Then He made from it its spouse﴾, and what does it give of the meaning of delay? I say: they are two signs from among the signs He enumerated, indicating His oneness and His power. This wonder of being split from the very self of Adam, and His creating Hawwa' from his rib (qusayra), are two matters; however, the one He made a continuous custom, while the other was not established as a custom, and no female other than Hawwa' was created from a man. So it was more fitting for it to be a sign and more striking to the wonder of the listener. He therefore joined it with 'thumma' to the first sign, to indicate its distinction in excellence and merit, and its delay from it in what returns to the increase of its being a sign. So it is a delay in status and rank, not a delay in existence." End of quotation.

As for ﴿Then He made from it its spouse﴾, the discussion of this "making" has already preceded at the beginning of Surah al-Nisa'.

The description of the livestock as "sent down" (inzal) is metaphorical, either because their provisions are described as descending from the sky, since everything that will exist is written in the Preserved Tablet, or because they subsist on plants, and plants arise from rain, and rain descends from the sky; so it is as if He sent them down. This is like the saying of the poet:

"The humps of the camels in its rain-cloud (rabab)"

meaning: in its cloud. Another said:

"The sop has been placed upon the heads of the sticks"

It was also said: He created them in Paradise and then sent them down; according to this, the sending down of their roots is literal.

Al-an'am (livestock): camels, cattle, sheep and goats. "Eight pairs" because each of them is male and female, and a zawj (pair) is what has another of its kind with it; when it stands alone it is a fard (single) and witr (odd). The Exalted said: ﴿So He made from it the two spouses, the male and the female﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 39].

Ibn Zayd said: ﴿creation after creation﴾ means another from the back of Adam and the backs of the fathers. Ikrimah, Mujahid and al-Suddi said: stages, ﴿creation after creation﴾, such as the lump of flesh, the clot and other than these.

Al-Zamakhshari took it up and said: a complete living being after bones clothed with flesh, after bare bones, after the chewed lump, after the clot, after the drop. End of quotation.

Isa and Talhah read ﴿yakhluqukum﴾ with the qaf assimilated into the kaf (idgham).

The three darknesses (al-zulumat al-thalath): the belly, the womb and the amniotic membrane (al-mashimah). It was also said: the loins (al-sulb), the womb and the belly.

﴿That﴾ (dhalikum): a reference to the One characterized by those previously mentioned attributes, from the creation of the heavens and what follows that of acts.

﴿Then how are you turned away?﴾ meaning: how do you turn away from worshipping Him to worshipping other than Him?

﴿If you disbelieve﴾: Ibn Abbas said: it is addressed to the disbelievers whose hearts God did not will to purify. "His servants" are the believers. This is supported by His saying before it: "Then how are you turned away?", and this is for the disbelievers, so "If you disbelieve" came as an address to them. ﴿Indeed God is free of need of you﴾, and of your worship, since no benefit returns to Him from you nor from your worship, for He is the Absolutely Self-Sufficient. Ibn Atiyyah said: it is possible that it addresses all people, because He, exalted is He, is free of need of all of them, while they are needy of Him. End of quotation.

The expression "His servants" is general. It was said: the intended meaning is particular, namely the angels and the believing humans and jinn. "Ridha" (pleasure/approval) here means "irada" (will), so according to this it is an attribute of essence. It was also said: the intended meaning is generality, as the wording indicates, and ridha is different from irada; it is expressed by it to mean gratitude and reward, i.e., He does not approve for them a religion nor reward them with good by it. So ridha according to this is an attribute of act, in the sense of acceptance and reward.

Ibn Atiyyah said: Consider irada, for its reality is only in what has not yet occurred, while ridha's reality is only in what has already occurred; reflect on this in the verses of the Qur'an and you will find it, though the Arabs may use one in place of the other in their poetry by way of metaphor.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Some deviants have strained to attribute to God what He has negated of His essence, namely approval of disbelief for His servants, and said: this is from the general that is intended to be particular, and He did not intend except His servants whom He meant in His saying: "Indeed My servants, you have no authority over them" [al-Hijr: 42], meaning the protected ones, due to His saying: "a spring from which God's servants drink" [al-Insan: 6]. Exalted is God above what the wrongdoers say. End of quotation.

Thus he called ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbbas, the interpreter of the Qur'an, and the leading scholars of the Sunnah, "some deviants," and applied to them the name of wrongdoers, and that is from his foolishness and audacity, as I said in my qasida in which I mentioned what is to be criticized in it:

"He insults the leading imams with misguidance, especially if they have entered him into narrow straits."

﴿And if you give thanks, He is pleased with it for you﴾: Ibn Abbas said: He multiplies it for you, and it seems he means the reward of gratitude; it was also said: He accepts it from you. The author of al-Tahrir said: The strength of the speech indicates that the meaning of "you give thanks" is "you believe," until it stands opposite to disbelief; and God Exalted has named righteous deeds and acts of obedience "thanks" in His saying: ﴿Work, family of Dawud, in thanks﴾ [Saba': 13]. End of quotation.

The discussion of this verse has already preceded in Saba'.

Al-Nahwiyyan (the two grammarians, Abu Amr and al-Kisa'i) and Ibn Kathir read ﴿yardahu﴾ by connecting the damma of the ha' to a waw; Ibn Amir and Hafs read with a damma only; Abu Bakr read with a sukun on the ha'. Abu Hatim said: this is an error and not permissible. End of quotation.

It is not an error; rather, that is a dialect of the Banu Kilab and Banu ʿUqayl. As for His saying: "and no bearer bears the burden of another" up to "the contents of the breasts," its discussion has already preceded.

(p. 418) **Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 39, verses 8–16 (part 1 of 2)**

﴿When harm touches man, he calls upon his Lord, turning to Him in repentance. Then, when He grants him a blessing from Himself, he forgets what he had been calling upon Him for before, and he sets up rivals to God so that he may lead (others) astray from His way. Say: "Enjoy your disbelief for a little while; indeed you are among the companions of the Fire."﴾ ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night, prostrating and standing (in prayer), fearing the Hereafter and hoping for the mercy of his Lord (like one who does not)? Say: "Are those who know equal to those who do not know?" Only people of understanding are mindful.﴾ ﴿Say: "O My servants who believe, fear your Lord. For those who do good in this world there is good, and God's earth is spacious. Indeed the patient will be given their reward without measure."﴾ ﴿Say: "I have been commanded to worship God, making my religion sincerely His."﴾ ﴿"And I have been commanded to be the first of those who submit."﴾ ﴿Say: "Indeed I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a tremendous Day."﴾ ﴿Say: "God I worship, making my religion sincerely His."﴾ ﴿"So worship what you will besides Him." Say: "Indeed the losers are those who have lost themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection. Is that not the clear loss?"﴾ ﴿"For them there will be layers of Fire above them and layers below them. This is what God frightens His servants with. O My servants, then fear Me."﴾

The apparent meaning is that "man" (al-insan) here refers to the category of the disbeliever. It has also been said that it refers to a specific person, such as Utba ibn Rabi'a. "Harm" (al-durr) includes all kinds of hardship, whether in body, family or property.

﴿He calls upon his Lord﴾: he seeks refuge with his Lord and calls out to Him, hoping for no one else to remove the harm. ﴿turning to Him in repentance﴾ means returning to Him alone for the removal of that harm.

﴿Then, when He grants him﴾: He bestows and gives him, after the removal of that harm. The literal meaning of khawwalahu (He granted him) is derived from their saying "he is his khawwil," meaning one who takes good care of him. Or it is derived from khala yakhulu, meaning to strut and boast. The Arabs say:

*"Indeed the wealthy man, long of train, swaggering."*

﴿He forgets what he had been calling upon﴾ means he abandons it. The apparent meaning is that ma is in the sense of alladhi ("that which"), i.e., he forgets the harm for which he had been calling God to remove. It has also been said that ma is in the sense of man ("who"), i.e., he forgets his Lord whom he used to beseech humbly and implore to remove his harm. It has also been said that ma is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyya), i.e., he forgets that he was calling.

It has been said that the sentence is complete at His saying "forgets," meaning he forgets what harm he was in. Here ma is negative, denying that this disbeliever's supplication was sincerely for God alone, confined to the time of harm. According to the preceding opinions, (min qabl) means "before," i.e., before the granting of the blessing, which is the time of harm.

﴿And sets up rivals to God﴾: i.e., equals that oppose and contradict one another. Qatada said: that is, men whom they obey in disobedience. Others said: idols. This is from the foolishness of their minds: when harm touched them, they called upon God and did not seek refuge in anything but Him for its removal; when that was removed and the blessing was granted, they associated others with Him. Thus the lam (in liyudilla) is the lam of cause (purpose), and it has been said it is the lam of consequence (result). The majority read liyudilla with a *damma* on the *ya'*, meaning that he was not content with his own misguidance until he made others go astray. Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr and Isa read it with a *fatha* on the *ya'*. Then He used the imperative form, saying: ﴿Enjoy your disbelief for a little while﴾, i.e., take pleasure and do what you wish for a little while, meaning a brief lifespan. The address is to the disbeliever who sets up rivals to God.

﴿Indeed you are among the companions of the Fire﴾: i.e., among its residents who will abide therein forever. Al-Zamakhshari said: His saying ﴿Enjoy your disbelief﴾ is in the manner of abandonment and leaving (him to himself), as if it were said to him: since you refused before what you were commanded of faith and obedience, it is right that you not be commanded to it after that. He is commanded to leave it as an intensification of his abandonment, being left to himself and his affairs, for there is no greater abandonment than being sent in the opposite direction of what they were commanded. A parallel in meaning is: ﴿A little enjoyment, then their refuge is Hell﴾ [Al 'Imran: 197]. End of quote.

When He explained some of the circumstances of the wrongdoers, the misguided polytheists, He followed it with an explanation of the circumstances of those who are guided and who affirm God's oneness, saying: ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Hamza, al-A'mash, Isa, Shayba and al-Hasan in one narration read *amman* with a lightened *mim*. The apparent reading is that the hamza is an interrogative of affirmation, and its counterpart is omitted because the meaning is understood. The estimated sense is: "Is this devout one better, or the disbeliever addressed in His saying: 'Enjoy your disbelief'?" His saying "Are those who know equal to those who do not know" indicates this. Among the omission of the counterpart is the poet's verse:

*"The heart called me to her; indeed I am obedient to her command, yet I do not know whether pursuing her is rectitude."*

The estimated sense is: "or is it error?"

Al-Farra' said: the hamza is for calling, as if it were said: "O you who is devoutly obedient," and His saying "Say" would be an address to him. This view is remote from what precedes and follows it. Abu Ali al-Farisi weakened this view, and no attention is paid to the weakening of this reading by al-Akhfash and Abu Hatim. The rest of the seven readers, al-Hasan, Qatada, al-A'raj and Abu Ja'far read *amman* with a doubled *mim*. Here *am* has been assimilated into the *mim* of *man*. Thus *am* may be connected, with its counterpart omitted before it. Its estimated sense is: "Is this disbeliever better, or the one who is devoutly obedient?" Al-Akhfash said this is its meaning. Such an estimation requires a hearing from the Arabs, namely that the first counterpart be omitted.

*Am* may also be disconnected, being estimated as *bal* with the hamza, so the sense is: "Rather, is the one who is devoutly obedient, whose attribute is such, like one who is not such?" Al-Nahhas said: *am* means *bal* ("rather"), and *man* means *alladhi* ("the one who"), and the estimated sense is: "Rather, the one who is devoutly obedient is better than the one mentioned before him." End of quote.

But there is no superiority to the one before him so that this could be made superior. Rather, the predicate is estimated as "from the companions of Paradise," indicated by its counterpart: ﴿Indeed you are among the companions of the Fire﴾. The *qanit* (devoutly obedient) means obedient, as Ibn Abbas said. The discussion of *qunut* has already been covered in Surat al-Baqara.

The majority read ﴿prostrating and standing﴾ with *nasb* (accusative) as circumstantial states (hal). Al-Dahhak read them with *raf'* (nominative), either as a description of *qanit*, or as a predicate after a predicate. The *waw* serves to join the two attributes.

﴿Fearing the Hereafter﴾, i.e., the punishment of the Hereafter. ﴿hoping for the mercy of his Lord﴾, i.e., its attainment. It has also been said: the bliss of Paradise. This one who is characterised by devotion, along with the other attributes, was said by Muqatil to be Ammar, Suhayb, Ibn Mas'ud and Abu Dharr. Ibn Umar said it was Uthman. Ibn Abbas, in a narration from al-Dahhak, said it was Abu Bakr and Umar. Yahya ibn Salam said it was the Messenger of God (ﷺ). The apparent meaning is that it applies to whoever is characterised by these attributes, without specifying a particular person.

In the verse there is evidence for the excellence of the night prayer, and that it is more meritorious than the prayer of the day.

When He mentioned the deed, He mentioned knowledge, saying: ﴿Say: "Are those who know equal to those who do not know?"﴾ This indicates that human perfection is confined to these two aims. Just as these two are not equal, so the obedient and the disobedient are not equal. The knowledge meant here is that which leads to knowing God and to the servant's salvation from His wrath. He read *yadhdhakkaru* (with the doubled *dhal*) by assimilating the *ta'* of *yatadhakkaru* into the *dhal*.

﴿Say: "O My servants who believe, fear your Lord"﴾. It is narrated that it was revealed concerning Ja'far ibn Abi Talib and his companions when they resolved to emigrate to the land of Abyssinia. God promised them, saying: ﴿For those who do good in this world there is good﴾. The apparent reading is that *fi hadhihi* ("in this") is connected to *ahsanu* ("did good"), and that those who do good in this world will have good in the Hereafter, i.e., great good, which is Paradise, as Muqatil said. The qualifier is omitted, indicated by the meaning, because whoever does good in this world is not promised merely any good in the Hereafter. Al-Suddi said: *fi hadhihi* is a complement of *hasana* ("good"), meaning that if it had been placed after it, it would have been a description, i.e., those who do good, for them is a good existing in this world. Since it precedes, it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state. The good they have in this world is well-being, victory and God's protection.

Then He urged emigration, saying: ﴿And God's earth is spacious﴾, like His saying: ﴿Was not God's earth spacious so that you could emigrate therein?﴾ [An-Nisa': 97]. That is, there is absolutely no excuse for those who neglect, even if they plead their homelands, and that they cannot perform acts of obedience there. It is said to them: God's lands are many and spacious, so move to places where acts of obedience are possible for you.

'Ata said: ﴿God's earth﴾ is Medina for emigration. It was said: according to this, *ahsanu* means "emigrated," and *hasana* means relief from enemies.

Some people said: "God's earth" here means Paradise. Ibn Atiyya said: this view is arbitrary, with no evidence for it. End of quote.

Abu Muslim said: there is no impediment to that, because He commanded the believers to be mindful of God, then explained that for whoever is mindful there is good in the Hereafter, which is eternal abiding in Paradise; then He explained that God's earth is spacious, by His saying: ﴿And they will inherit the earth, to dwell in Paradise wherever they wish﴾ [Az-Zumar: 74], and His saying: ﴿A Garden whose width is the heavens and the earth, prepared for the God-fearing﴾ [Al 'Imran: 133].

Since the rank of excellence (ihsan) is the highest of ranks, as is reported in the hadith: "What is ihsan?" He said: "That you worship God as if you see Him." And since patience in that is among the most difficult things, especially for one who has left his homeland and kin and endured the trials of exile, He mentioned that the patient will be given their rewards without measure, i.e., they will not be reckoned in the Hereafter as others are reckoned; or they will be given what no reckoning can encompass in abundance.

﴿Say: "I have been commanded to worship God, making my religion sincerely His"﴾: God commanded him to proclaim openly to the disbelievers what he had been commanded of worshipping God, purifying it from impurities. (Wa umirtu) means: I have been commanded with what I was commanded, ﴿so that I may be the first of those who submit﴾, i.e., who submit to God, and by "first" he means among the people of his age or among his people, since he was the first to oppose the idol-worshippers, or the first whom he called to Islam as Islam, or the first who called his own soul to what he called others to, so that he may be followed by his words and deeds, unlike the kings who command what they do not do, or that he should do what entitles him to the status of first among the earlier ones, as an indication of the cause through the effect. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, how is *umirtu* ("I was commanded") coordinated with *umirtu* when they are the same? I say: they are not the same, because their aspects differ. The command to sincerity and its imposition is one thing, and the command to it so that one may win the prize of precedence in religion is another. When the two aspects and attributes of a thing differ, they are treated as two different things. You may also consider the lam to be extra, like its counterpart in *aradtu*, because *af'ala* is not extended with *lam* except with *an* specifically, not with a plain noun. It is as if it were added as a substitute for the omission of the original form in favour of what stands in its place, just as the sin was added to *istata'a* as a substitute for the omission of the original which is *atwa'*. The evidence for this view is that it comes without the lam in his saying: "And I have been commanded to be the first of those who submit." End of quote.

It is possible that in "that I be" (an akun) in the three places the original is "li-an akuna" (in order that I be), so the lam has been deleted; and the thing commanded is omitted, which is what is stated here: ﴿Indeed I have been commanded to worship God﴾.

﴿Say: "Indeed I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a tremendous Day"﴾: The discussion of this sentence, the content of the saying, has already been given in Surat Yunus.

When He first commanded him to inform that he had been commanded to worship God, He commanded him a second time to inform that he worships God alone. The mention of the Divine Name (al-Jalala) indicates concern with whom is worshipped. According to al-Zamakhshari, it indicates exclusivity. He said: For this indication, he placed the object of worship before the verb of worship, and delayed it in the first. So the first statement is about the act itself and its bringing about, and the second is about the one for whose sake the act is performed. For this reason His saying is ordered upon it: ﴿So worship what you will besides Him﴾. The command in this form, given as a matter of choice, means intensifying abandonment and leaving him to himself. End of quote.

Others said: ﴿So worship what you will﴾ is an imperative form in the manner of threat, in response to His saying: ﴿Say: "Enjoy your disbelief"﴾.

Qul inna al-khasirin ("Say: Indeed, the losers") — i.e., the reality of loss (al-khusran): (alladhina khasiru) — that is, they are the ones who lost themselves, since they have become among the people of the Fire, and their families (ahliyhim) who were with them in the world, since they will be with them in the Fire, so they will benefit nothing from them, even if their families had believed. Their loss of them is that they will not gather with them nor return to them.

Qatada said: "It is as if Allah had prepared for them families in Paradise, and they lost them." Maymun ibn Mihran said the same meaning. Al-Hasan said: "They are the wide-eyed houris (al-hur al-'in)."

Then He mentioned that loss and emphasized it, first by alerting to it and pointing to it, and by stressing it with the verb, by defining it with the article (al-), and by describing it as al-mubin, meaning clear to anyone who reflects upon it even slightly.

When He mentioned their loss of themselves and their families, He mentioned their condition in Jahannam, and that above them are canopies (zulal) and below them are canopies, showing that the Fire envelops them from above and from below. He called what is beneath them "canopies" to match what is above them, as He said: ﴿On the Day the punishment will cover them from above them and from beneath their feet﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 55], and He said to them: ﴿From Jahannam is a bed, and above them are coverings﴾ [al-A'raf: 41]. It has also been said: they are canopies for those who are beneath them, since the Fire has layers (tibaq). It has also been said: what is beneath them blazes, and something from it rises up until it becomes a canopy, so it is called a canopy in consideration of what it ultimately becomes.

(Dhalika) — that is, that punishment, with which Allah frightens His servants, so that they may know what saves them from it. Then He called them and commanded them, saying: ﴿O My servants, so fear Me﴾ — that is, fear My punishment.
