(p. 418) **Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 39, verses 8–16 (part 1 of 2)**

﴿When harm touches man, he calls upon his Lord, turning to Him in repentance. Then, when He grants him a blessing from Himself, he forgets what he had been calling upon Him for before, and he sets up rivals to God so that he may lead (others) astray from His way. Say: "Enjoy your disbelief for a little while; indeed you are among the companions of the Fire."﴾ ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night, prostrating and standing (in prayer), fearing the Hereafter and hoping for the mercy of his Lord (like one who does not)? Say: "Are those who know equal to those who do not know?" Only people of understanding are mindful.﴾ ﴿Say: "O My servants who believe, fear your Lord. For those who do good in this world there is good, and God's earth is spacious. Indeed the patient will be given their reward without measure."﴾ ﴿Say: "I have been commanded to worship God, making my religion sincerely His."﴾ ﴿"And I have been commanded to be the first of those who submit."﴾ ﴿Say: "Indeed I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a tremendous Day."﴾ ﴿Say: "God I worship, making my religion sincerely His."﴾ ﴿"So worship what you will besides Him." Say: "Indeed the losers are those who have lost themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection. Is that not the clear loss?"﴾ ﴿"For them there will be layers of Fire above them and layers below them. This is what God frightens His servants with. O My servants, then fear Me."﴾

The apparent meaning is that "man" (al-insan) here refers to the category of the disbeliever. It has also been said that it refers to a specific person, such as Utba ibn Rabi'a. "Harm" (al-durr) includes all kinds of hardship, whether in body, family or property.

﴿He calls upon his Lord﴾: he seeks refuge with his Lord and calls out to Him, hoping for no one else to remove the harm. ﴿turning to Him in repentance﴾ means returning to Him alone for the removal of that harm.

﴿Then, when He grants him﴾: He bestows and gives him, after the removal of that harm. The literal meaning of khawwalahu (He granted him) is derived from their saying "he is his khawwil," meaning one who takes good care of him. Or it is derived from khala yakhulu, meaning to strut and boast. The Arabs say:

*"Indeed the wealthy man, long of train, swaggering."*

﴿He forgets what he had been calling upon﴾ means he abandons it. The apparent meaning is that ma is in the sense of alladhi ("that which"), i.e., he forgets the harm for which he had been calling God to remove. It has also been said that ma is in the sense of man ("who"), i.e., he forgets his Lord whom he used to beseech humbly and implore to remove his harm. It has also been said that ma is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyya), i.e., he forgets that he was calling.

It has been said that the sentence is complete at His saying "forgets," meaning he forgets what harm he was in. Here ma is negative, denying that this disbeliever's supplication was sincerely for God alone, confined to the time of harm. According to the preceding opinions, (min qabl) means "before," i.e., before the granting of the blessing, which is the time of harm.

﴿And sets up rivals to God﴾: i.e., equals that oppose and contradict one another. Qatada said: that is, men whom they obey in disobedience. Others said: idols. This is from the foolishness of their minds: when harm touched them, they called upon God and did not seek refuge in anything but Him for its removal; when that was removed and the blessing was granted, they associated others with Him. Thus the lam (in liyudilla) is the lam of cause (purpose), and it has been said it is the lam of consequence (result). The majority read liyudilla with a *damma* on the *ya'*, meaning that he was not content with his own misguidance until he made others go astray. Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr and Isa read it with a *fatha* on the *ya'*. Then He used the imperative form, saying: ﴿Enjoy your disbelief for a little while﴾, i.e., take pleasure and do what you wish for a little while, meaning a brief lifespan. The address is to the disbeliever who sets up rivals to God.

﴿Indeed you are among the companions of the Fire﴾: i.e., among its residents who will abide therein forever. Al-Zamakhshari said: His saying ﴿Enjoy your disbelief﴾ is in the manner of abandonment and leaving (him to himself), as if it were said to him: since you refused before what you were commanded of faith and obedience, it is right that you not be commanded to it after that. He is commanded to leave it as an intensification of his abandonment, being left to himself and his affairs, for there is no greater abandonment than being sent in the opposite direction of what they were commanded. A parallel in meaning is: ﴿A little enjoyment, then their refuge is Hell﴾ [Al 'Imran: 197]. End of quote.

When He explained some of the circumstances of the wrongdoers, the misguided polytheists, He followed it with an explanation of the circumstances of those who are guided and who affirm God's oneness, saying: ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Hamza, al-A'mash, Isa, Shayba and al-Hasan in one narration read *amman* with a lightened *mim*. The apparent reading is that the hamza is an interrogative of affirmation, and its counterpart is omitted because the meaning is understood. The estimated sense is: "Is this devout one better, or the disbeliever addressed in His saying: 'Enjoy your disbelief'?" His saying "Are those who know equal to those who do not know" indicates this. Among the omission of the counterpart is the poet's verse:

*"The heart called me to her; indeed I am obedient to her command, yet I do not know whether pursuing her is rectitude."*

The estimated sense is: "or is it error?"

Al-Farra' said: the hamza is for calling, as if it were said: "O you who is devoutly obedient," and His saying "Say" would be an address to him. This view is remote from what precedes and follows it. Abu Ali al-Farisi weakened this view, and no attention is paid to the weakening of this reading by al-Akhfash and Abu Hatim. The rest of the seven readers, al-Hasan, Qatada, al-A'raj and Abu Ja'far read *amman* with a doubled *mim*. Here *am* has been assimilated into the *mim* of *man*. Thus *am* may be connected, with its counterpart omitted before it. Its estimated sense is: "Is this disbeliever better, or the one who is devoutly obedient?" Al-Akhfash said this is its meaning. Such an estimation requires a hearing from the Arabs, namely that the first counterpart be omitted.

*Am* may also be disconnected, being estimated as *bal* with the hamza, so the sense is: "Rather, is the one who is devoutly obedient, whose attribute is such, like one who is not such?" Al-Nahhas said: *am* means *bal* ("rather"), and *man* means *alladhi* ("the one who"), and the estimated sense is: "Rather, the one who is devoutly obedient is better than the one mentioned before him." End of quote.

But there is no superiority to the one before him so that this could be made superior. Rather, the predicate is estimated as "from the companions of Paradise," indicated by its counterpart: ﴿Indeed you are among the companions of the Fire﴾. The *qanit* (devoutly obedient) means obedient, as Ibn Abbas said. The discussion of *qunut* has already been covered in Surat al-Baqara.

The majority read ﴿prostrating and standing﴾ with *nasb* (accusative) as circumstantial states (hal). Al-Dahhak read them with *raf'* (nominative), either as a description of *qanit*, or as a predicate after a predicate. The *waw* serves to join the two attributes.

﴿Fearing the Hereafter﴾, i.e., the punishment of the Hereafter. ﴿hoping for the mercy of his Lord﴾, i.e., its attainment. It has also been said: the bliss of Paradise. This one who is characterised by devotion, along with the other attributes, was said by Muqatil to be Ammar, Suhayb, Ibn Mas'ud and Abu Dharr. Ibn Umar said it was Uthman. Ibn Abbas, in a narration from al-Dahhak, said it was Abu Bakr and Umar. Yahya ibn Salam said it was the Messenger of God (ﷺ). The apparent meaning is that it applies to whoever is characterised by these attributes, without specifying a particular person.

In the verse there is evidence for the excellence of the night prayer, and that it is more meritorious than the prayer of the day.

When He mentioned the deed, He mentioned knowledge, saying: ﴿Say: "Are those who know equal to those who do not know?"﴾ This indicates that human perfection is confined to these two aims. Just as these two are not equal, so the obedient and the disobedient are not equal. The knowledge meant here is that which leads to knowing God and to the servant's salvation from His wrath. He read *yadhdhakkaru* (with the doubled *dhal*) by assimilating the *ta'* of *yatadhakkaru* into the *dhal*.

﴿Say: "O My servants who believe, fear your Lord"﴾. It is narrated that it was revealed concerning Ja'far ibn Abi Talib and his companions when they resolved to emigrate to the land of Abyssinia. God promised them, saying: ﴿For those who do good in this world there is good﴾. The apparent reading is that *fi hadhihi* ("in this") is connected to *ahsanu* ("did good"), and that those who do good in this world will have good in the Hereafter, i.e., great good, which is Paradise, as Muqatil said. The qualifier is omitted, indicated by the meaning, because whoever does good in this world is not promised merely any good in the Hereafter. Al-Suddi said: *fi hadhihi* is a complement of *hasana* ("good"), meaning that if it had been placed after it, it would have been a description, i.e., those who do good, for them is a good existing in this world. Since it precedes, it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state. The good they have in this world is well-being, victory and God's protection.

Then He urged emigration, saying: ﴿And God's earth is spacious﴾, like His saying: ﴿Was not God's earth spacious so that you could emigrate therein?﴾ [An-Nisa': 97]. That is, there is absolutely no excuse for those who neglect, even if they plead their homelands, and that they cannot perform acts of obedience there. It is said to them: God's lands are many and spacious, so move to places where acts of obedience are possible for you.

'Ata said: ﴿God's earth﴾ is Medina for emigration. It was said: according to this, *ahsanu* means "emigrated," and *hasana* means relief from enemies.

Some people said: "God's earth" here means Paradise. Ibn Atiyya said: this view is arbitrary, with no evidence for it. End of quote.

Abu Muslim said: there is no impediment to that, because He commanded the believers to be mindful of God, then explained that for whoever is mindful there is good in the Hereafter, which is eternal abiding in Paradise; then He explained that God's earth is spacious, by His saying: ﴿And they will inherit the earth, to dwell in Paradise wherever they wish﴾ [Az-Zumar: 74], and His saying: ﴿A Garden whose width is the heavens and the earth, prepared for the God-fearing﴾ [Al 'Imran: 133].

Since the rank of excellence (ihsan) is the highest of ranks, as is reported in the hadith: "What is ihsan?" He said: "That you worship God as if you see Him." And since patience in that is among the most difficult things, especially for one who has left his homeland and kin and endured the trials of exile, He mentioned that the patient will be given their rewards without measure, i.e., they will not be reckoned in the Hereafter as others are reckoned; or they will be given what no reckoning can encompass in abundance.

﴿Say: "I have been commanded to worship God, making my religion sincerely His"﴾: God commanded him to proclaim openly to the disbelievers what he had been commanded of worshipping God, purifying it from impurities. (Wa umirtu) means: I have been commanded with what I was commanded, ﴿so that I may be the first of those who submit﴾, i.e., who submit to God, and by "first" he means among the people of his age or among his people, since he was the first to oppose the idol-worshippers, or the first whom he called to Islam as Islam, or the first who called his own soul to what he called others to, so that he may be followed by his words and deeds, unlike the kings who command what they do not do, or that he should do what entitles him to the status of first among the earlier ones, as an indication of the cause through the effect. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, how is *umirtu* ("I was commanded") coordinated with *umirtu* when they are the same? I say: they are not the same, because their aspects differ. The command to sincerity and its imposition is one thing, and the command to it so that one may win the prize of precedence in religion is another. When the two aspects and attributes of a thing differ, they are treated as two different things. You may also consider the lam to be extra, like its counterpart in *aradtu*, because *af'ala* is not extended with *lam* except with *an* specifically, not with a plain noun. It is as if it were added as a substitute for the omission of the original form in favour of what stands in its place, just as the sin was added to *istata'a* as a substitute for the omission of the original which is *atwa'*. The evidence for this view is that it comes without the lam in his saying: "And I have been commanded to be the first of those who submit." End of quote.

It is possible that in "that I be" (an akun) in the three places the original is "li-an akuna" (in order that I be), so the lam has been deleted; and the thing commanded is omitted, which is what is stated here: ﴿Indeed I have been commanded to worship God﴾.

﴿Say: "Indeed I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a tremendous Day"﴾: The discussion of this sentence, the content of the saying, has already been given in Surat Yunus.

When He first commanded him to inform that he had been commanded to worship God, He commanded him a second time to inform that he worships God alone. The mention of the Divine Name (al-Jalala) indicates concern with whom is worshipped. According to al-Zamakhshari, it indicates exclusivity. He said: For this indication, he placed the object of worship before the verb of worship, and delayed it in the first. So the first statement is about the act itself and its bringing about, and the second is about the one for whose sake the act is performed. For this reason His saying is ordered upon it: ﴿So worship what you will besides Him﴾. The command in this form, given as a matter of choice, means intensifying abandonment and leaving him to himself. End of quote.

Others said: ﴿So worship what you will﴾ is an imperative form in the manner of threat, in response to His saying: ﴿Say: "Enjoy your disbelief"﴾.

Qul inna al-khasirin ("Say: Indeed, the losers") — i.e., the reality of loss (al-khusran): (alladhina khasiru) — that is, they are the ones who lost themselves, since they have become among the people of the Fire, and their families (ahliyhim) who were with them in the world, since they will be with them in the Fire, so they will benefit nothing from them, even if their families had believed. Their loss of them is that they will not gather with them nor return to them.

Qatada said: "It is as if Allah had prepared for them families in Paradise, and they lost them." Maymun ibn Mihran said the same meaning. Al-Hasan said: "They are the wide-eyed houris (al-hur al-'in)."

Then He mentioned that loss and emphasized it, first by alerting to it and pointing to it, and by stressing it with the verb, by defining it with the article (al-), and by describing it as al-mubin, meaning clear to anyone who reflects upon it even slightly.

When He mentioned their loss of themselves and their families, He mentioned their condition in Jahannam, and that above them are canopies (zulal) and below them are canopies, showing that the Fire envelops them from above and from below. He called what is beneath them "canopies" to match what is above them, as He said: ﴿On the Day the punishment will cover them from above them and from beneath their feet﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 55], and He said to them: ﴿From Jahannam is a bed, and above them are coverings﴾ [al-A'raf: 41]. It has also been said: they are canopies for those who are beneath them, since the Fire has layers (tibaq). It has also been said: what is beneath them blazes, and something from it rises up until it becomes a canopy, so it is called a canopy in consideration of what it ultimately becomes.

(Dhalika) — that is, that punishment, with which Allah frightens His servants, so that they may know what saves them from it. Then He called them and commanded them, saying: ﴿O My servants, so fear Me﴾ — that is, fear My punishment.

Then He urged emigration, saying: ﴿And God's earth is spacious﴾, like His saying: ﴿Was not God's earth spacious so that you could emigrate therein?﴾ [An-Nisa': 97]. That is, there is absolutely no excuse for those who neglect, even if they plead their homelands, and that they cannot perform acts of obedience there. It is said to them: God's lands are many and spacious, so move to places where acts of obedience are possible for you.

'Ata said: ﴿God's earth﴾ is Medina for emigration. It was said: according to this, *ahsanu* means "emigrated," and *hasana* means relief from enemies.

Some people said: "God's earth" here means Paradise. Ibn Atiyya said: this view is arbitrary, with no evidence for it. End of quote.

Abu Muslim said: there is no impediment to that, because He commanded the believers to be mindful of God, then explained that for whoever is mindful there is good in the Hereafter, which is eternal abiding in Paradise; then He explained that God's earth is spacious, by His saying: ﴿And they will inherit the earth, to dwell in Paradise wherever they wish﴾ [Az-Zumar: 74], and His saying: ﴿A Garden whose width is the heavens and the earth, prepared for the God-fearing﴾ [Al 'Imran: 133].

Others said: ﴿So worship what you will﴾ is an imperative form in the manner of threat, in response to His saying: ﴿Say: "Enjoy your disbelief"﴾.

The apparent reading is that the hamza is an interrogative of affirmation, and its counterpart is omitted because the meaning is understood. The estimated sense is: "Is this devout one better, or the disbeliever addressed in His saying: 'Enjoy your disbelief'?" His saying "Are those who know equal to those who do not know" indicates this. Among the omission of the counterpart is the poet's verse:

*"The heart called me to her; indeed I am obedient to her command, yet I do not know whether pursuing her is rectitude."*

The estimated sense is: "or is it error?"

Al-Farra' said: the hamza is for calling, as if it were said: "O you who is devoutly obedient," and His saying "Say" would be an address to him. This view is remote from what precedes and follows it. Abu Ali al-Farisi weakened this view, and no attention is paid to the weakening of this reading by al-Akhfash and Abu Hatim. The rest of the seven readers, al-Hasan, Qatada, al-A'raj and Abu Ja'far read *amman* with a doubled *mim*. Here *am* has been assimilated into the *mim* of *man*. Thus *am* may be connected, with its counterpart omitted before it. Its estimated sense is: "Is this disbeliever better, or the one who is devoutly obedient?" Al-Akhfash said this is its meaning. Such an estimation requires a hearing from the Arabs, namely that the first counterpart be omitted.

*Am* may also be disconnected, being estimated as *bal* with the hamza, so the sense is: "Rather, is the one who is devoutly obedient, whose attribute is such, like one who is not such?" Al-Nahhas said: *am* means *bal* ("rather"), and *man* means *alladhi* ("the one who"), and the estimated sense is: "Rather, the one who is devoutly obedient is better than the one mentioned before him." End of quote.

But there is no superiority to the one before him so that this could be made superior. Rather, the predicate is estimated as "from the companions of Paradise," indicated by its counterpart: ﴿Indeed you are among the companions of the Fire﴾. The *qanit* (devoutly obedient) means obedient, as Ibn Abbas said. The discussion of *qunut* has already been covered in Surat al-Baqara.

The majority read ﴿prostrating and standing﴾ with *nasb* (accusative) as circumstantial states (hal). Al-Dahhak read them with *raf'* (nominative), either as a description of *qanit*, or as a predicate after a predicate. The *waw* serves to join the two attributes.

﴿Fearing the Hereafter﴾, i.e., the punishment of the Hereafter. ﴿hoping for the mercy of his Lord﴾, i.e., its attainment. It has also been said: the bliss of Paradise. This one who is characterised by devotion, along with the other attributes, was said by Muqatil to be Ammar, Suhayb, Ibn Mas'ud and Abu Dharr. Ibn Umar said it was Uthman. Ibn Abbas, in a narration from al-Dahhak, said it was Abu Bakr and Umar. Yahya ibn Salam said it was the Messenger of God (ﷺ). The apparent meaning is that it applies to whoever is characterised by these attributes, without specifying a particular person.

In the verse there is evidence for the excellence of the night prayer, and that it is more meritorious than the prayer of the day.

When He mentioned the deed, He mentioned knowledge, saying: ﴿Say: "Are those who know equal to those who do not know?"﴾ This indicates that human perfection is confined to these two aims. Just as these two are not equal, so the obedient and the disobedient are not equal. The knowledge meant here is that which leads to knowing God and to the servant's salvation from His wrath. He read *yadhdhakkaru* (with the doubled *dhal*) by assimilating the *ta'* of *yatadhakkaru* into the *dhal*.

﴿Say: "O My servants who believe, fear your Lord"﴾. It is narrated that it was revealed concerning Ja'far ibn Abi Talib and his companions when they resolved to emigrate to the land of Abyssinia. God promised them, saying: ﴿For those who do good in this world there is good﴾. The apparent reading is that *fi hadhihi* ("in this") is connected to *ahsanu* ("did good"), and that those who do good in this world will have good in the Hereafter, i.e., great good, which is Paradise, as Muqatil said. The qualifier is omitted, indicated by the meaning, because whoever does good in this world is not promised merely any good in the Hereafter. Al-Suddi said: *fi hadhihi* is a complement of *hasana* ("good"), meaning that if it had been placed after it, it would have been a description, i.e., those who do good, for them is a good existing in this world. Since it precedes, it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state. The good they have in this world is well-being, victory and God's protection.

Then He urged emigration, saying: ﴿And God's earth is spacious﴾, like His saying: ﴿Was not God's earth spacious so that you could emigrate therein?﴾ [An-Nisa': 97]. That is, there is absolutely no excuse for those who neglect, even if they plead their homelands, and that they cannot perform acts of obedience there. It is said to them: God's lands are many and spacious, so move to places where acts of obedience are possible for you.

'Ata said: ﴿God's earth﴾ is Medina for emigration. It was said: according to this, *ahsanu* means "emigrated," and *hasana* means relief from enemies.

Some people said: "God's earth" here means Paradise. Ibn Atiyya said: this view is arbitrary, with no evidence for it. End of quote.

Abu Muslim said: there is no impediment to that, because He commanded the believers to be mindful of God, then explained that for whoever is mindful there is good in the Hereafter, which is eternal abiding in Paradise; then He explained that God's earth is spacious, by His saying: ﴿And they will inherit the earth, to dwell in Paradise wherever they wish﴾ [Az-Zumar: 74], and His saying: ﴿A Garden whose width is the heavens and the earth, prepared for the God-fearing﴾ [Al 'Imran: 133].

Since the rank of excellence (ihsan) is the highest of ranks, as is reported in the hadith: "What is ihsan?" He said: "That you worship God as if you see Him." And since patience in that is among the most difficult things, especially for one who has left his homeland and kin and endured the trials of exile, He mentioned that the patient will be given their rewards without measure, i.e., they will not be reckoned in the Hereafter as others are reckoned; or they will be given what no reckoning can encompass in abundance.

﴿Say: "I have been commanded to worship God, making my religion sincerely His"﴾: God commanded him to proclaim openly to the disbelievers what he had been commanded of worshipping God, purifying it from impurities. (Wa umirtu) means: I have been commanded with what I was commanded, ﴿so that I may be the first of those who submit﴾, i.e., who submit to God, and by "first" he means among the people of his age or among his people, since he was the first to oppose the idol-worshippers, or the first whom he called to Islam as Islam, or the first who called his own soul to what he called others to, so that he may be followed by his words and deeds, unlike the kings who command what they do not do, or that he should do what entitles him to the status of first among the earlier ones, as an indication of the cause through the effect. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, how is *umirtu* ("I was commanded") coordinated with *umirtu* when they are the same? I say: they are not the same, because their aspects differ. The command to sincerity and its imposition is one thing, and the command to it so that one may win the prize of precedence in religion is another. When the two aspects and attributes of a thing differ, they are treated as two different things. You may also consider the lam to be extra, like its counterpart in *aradtu*, because *af'ala* is not extended with *lam* except with *an* specifically, not with a plain noun. It is as if it were added as a substitute for the omission of the original form in favour of what stands in its place, just as the sin was added to *istata'a* as a substitute for the omission of the original which is *atwa'*. The evidence for this view is that it comes without the lam in his saying: "And I have been commanded to be the first of those who submit." End of quote.

It is possible that in "that I be" (an akun) in the three places the original is "li-an akuna" (in order that I be), so the lam has been deleted; and the thing commanded is omitted, which is what is stated here: ﴿Indeed I have been commanded to worship God﴾.

﴿Say: "Indeed I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a tremendous Day"﴾: The discussion of this sentence, the content of the saying, has already been given in Surat Yunus.

When He first commanded him to inform that he had been commanded to worship God, He commanded him a second time to inform that he worships God alone. The mention of the Divine Name (al-Jalala) indicates concern with whom is worshipped. According to al-Zamakhshari, it indicates exclusivity. He said: For this indication, he placed the object of worship before the verb of worship, and delayed it in the first. So the first statement is about the act itself and its bringing about, and the second is about the one for whose sake the act is performed. For this reason His saying is ordered upon it: ﴿So worship what you will besides Him﴾. The command in this form, given as a matter of choice, means intensifying abandonment and leaving him to himself. End of quote.

Others said: ﴿So worship what you will﴾ is an imperative form in the manner of threat, in response to His saying: ﴿Say: "Enjoy your disbelief"﴾.

Qul inna al-khasirin ("Say: Indeed, the losers") — i.e., the reality of loss (al-khusran): (alladhina khasiru) — that is, they are the ones who lost themselves, since they have become among the people of the Fire, and their families (ahliyhim) who were with them in the world, since they will be with them in the Fire, so they will benefit nothing from them, even if their families had believed. Their loss of them is that they will not gather with them nor return to them.

Qatada said: "It is as if Allah had prepared for them families in Paradise, and they lost them." Maymun ibn Mihran said the same meaning. Al-Hasan said: "They are the wide-eyed houris (al-hur al-'in)."

Then He mentioned that loss and emphasized it, first by alerting to it and pointing to it, and by stressing it with the verb, by defining it with the article (al-), and by describing it as al-mubin, meaning clear to anyone who reflects upon it even slightly.

When He mentioned their loss of themselves and their families, He mentioned their condition in Jahannam, and that above them are canopies (zulal) and below them are canopies, showing that the Fire envelops them from above and from below. He called what is beneath them "canopies" to match what is above them, as He said: ﴿On the Day the punishment will cover them from above them and from beneath their feet﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 55], and He said to them: ﴿From Jahannam is a bed, and above them are coverings﴾ [al-A'raf: 41]. It has also been said: they are canopies for those who are beneath them, since the Fire has layers (tibaq). It has also been said: what is beneath them blazes, and something from it rises up until it becomes a canopy, so it is called a canopy in consideration of what it ultimately becomes.

(Dhalika) — that is, that punishment, with which Allah frightens His servants, so that they may know what saves them from it. Then He called them and commanded them, saying: ﴿O My servants, so fear Me﴾ — that is, fear My punishment.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 39, verse 17–22:

(p-421) ﴿Those who avoid the Taghut (false deities), not worshipping them, and turn back in repentance to Allah — for them is good tidings. So give good tidings to My servants, ﴾ ﴿those who listen to the word and follow the best of it. Those are the ones whom Allah has guided, and those are the people of understanding.﴾ ﴿Is one against whom the word of punishment has become due [to be saved]? Would you then rescue those who are in the Fire?﴾ ﴿But those who fear their Lord — for them are upper chambers, built above upper chambers, beneath which rivers flow. It is the promise of Allah; Allah does not fail in His promise.﴾ ﴿Do you not see that Allah sends down water from the sky and makes it flow as springs in the earth, then brings out by it crops of varying colours, then it withers and you see it turn yellow, then He makes it into debris? Indeed in that is a reminder for people of understanding.﴾ ﴿Is one whose breast Allah has opened to Islam, so that he is upon a light from his Lord [like one who is hard-hearted]? Woe to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah. Those are in clear error.﴾

Ibn Zayd said: ﴿Those who avoid the Taghut﴾ was revealed concerning Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl, Salman, and Abu Dharr.

Ibn Ishaq said: The reference is to ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf, Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas, Saʿid ibn Zayd, and al-Zubayr. That is because when Abu Bakr embraced Islam, they heard of it and came to him and said: "Have you become a Muslim?" He said: "Yes," and he reminded them of Allah, so they all believed. Thus it was revealed concerning them, and it is muhkam (definitive in its ruling) for people until the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Taghut: the discussion of it has already passed in al-Baqarah. Al-Hasan recited (al-Tawaghit) in the plural.

﴿That they should not worship it﴾: i.e., its worship. It is a badal al-ishtimal (a substitution of inclusion).

(For them is good tidings): i.e., from Allah, the Exalted, of reward.

(So give good tidings to My servants): they are those who avoid the Taghut and turn to Allah. He placed the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun to indicate that they are indeed those, and so that the descriptive clause follows the apparent noun: ﴿those who listen to the word﴾, which is general over all sayings, ﴿and follow the best of it﴾: a praise of them for the penetration of their insight and their discernment of the best; so when they hear a saying, they examine it.

It was said: the best of speech is the Qur'an and what refers back to it. It was also said: the word is the Qur'an, and its best is what contains pardon, forgiveness, forbearance and the like. Qatadah said: the best of speech is obedience to Allah.

From Ibn ʿAbbas: it is the man who sits with a people, hears a discourse containing both good and bad, and relates the best of what he heard, and refrains from the rest.

(Alladhina) is a description of (ʿibad). It was also said: the pause is at ʿibad, and (alladhina) is a subject whose predicate is (ulaʾika) and what follows it.

﴿Is one against whom the word of punishment has become due﴾: it was said it was revealed concerning Abu Jahl, i.e., the threat of punishment was executed against him. The apparent view is that it is an independent sentence, and (man) is a relative subject whose predicate is omitted. It was said its estimate is: "he grieves over him," and it was said: "he seeks to free himself from him." Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as: "then you deliver him," saying: it is omitted because of the indication of ﴿Would you then rescue﴾ upon it. Al-Zamakhshari also estimated a clause between the hamzah and the fa', so that the hamzah and the fa' each remain in its place, saying: the estimate is: "Are you the master of their affair? Then [is] the one against whom the word of punishment has become due [to be saved]?" This is an opinion in which he stood alone, as far as we know.

What the grammarians say is that the fa' is for coordination, and its place is before the hamzah, but since the hamzah has the right of beginning the sentence, it was placed first; so the original, according to them, is: "fa-man haqqa 'alayhi." On the view that it is an independent sentence, his statement ﴿Would you then rescue those in the Fire?﴾ is a question of reproach, and the pronoun is placed first to indicate that you are not able to rescue him from the Fire; rather no one is able to do that except Allah. A group, among them al-Hawfi and al-Zamakhshari, held that man is conditional, and the answer of the condition is ﴿afa-anta﴾; the fa' is the fa' of the answer which entered upon the clause of the consequence, and the hamzah was repeated to emphasise the meaning of denial and remoteness; and (man fi al-nar), which is apparent, was placed in the position of the pronoun, since the original would be "tunqiduhu"; it was made explicit to publicise their state and to reveal the baseness of their stations. Al-Hawfi said: the interrogative alif was brought when the speech was long, for emphasis; had it not been long, it would not be permissible to bring it, because it is not proper in Arabic to bring the interrogative alif on the noun and another alif on the condition. The meaning of the speech is: "Would you then rescue him?" End.

On this view, an interrogative and a conditional are combined; according to the consensus that the hamzah has been moved forward from what comes after it, the disagreement between Sibawayh and Yunus arises: is the last clause the object of the question, or is it the answer of the condition? On al-Zamakhshari's estimate, the hamzah does not enter upon the conditional noun, so an interrogative and a conditional do not combine; because in his view the interrogative entered upon the omitted clause, which is: "Are you the master of their affair?" and "fa-man" is coordinated to that omitted clause; the conditional clause is coordinated upon the interrogative clause. The deserving of punishment is descended upon them, and they, in this world, are in the position of entering the Fire; and the effort of the Messenger, upon him be peace, in calling them to faith is in the position of rescuing them from the Fire.

When He mentioned the state of the disbelievers in the Fire, and that the losers have canopies of fire above them, He mentioned the state of the believers. The istidrak (contrast) was appropriate here, since it lies between the disbelievers and the believers, so He said: (But those who fear). In that is an exhortation to piety: for them are lofty chambers, above which are built lofty chambers, i.e., the construction of dwellings laid out upon the earth. The pronoun in (from beneath them) refers to both groups, i.e., from beneath the lower chambers and the upper chambers, there being no difference between their highest and lowest. (Promise of Allah) is put in the accusative as a verbal noun emphasising the content of the sentence before it, since it implies the meaning of promise.

(Do you not see): an address and a reproach to the listener, concerning what he should take as a lesson from the acts of Allah which show the passing away and dissolution of this world.

﴿Then He made it flow as springs﴾: i.e., He made it enter channels and fountains. The apparent view is that the water of the springs is from rainwater, which the earth retains and which emerges little by little.

﴿Then He brings out by it crops﴾: He mentions His favour upon us by which our livelihood is sustained.

(Of varying colours): of red, white and yellow; the word "crops" includes all that is sown, both staple and otherwise; or its varieties vary, of wheat, barley, sesame and other things.

(Then it withers): it approaches fruition; (then you see it yellow): i.e., its greenness and freshness have gone.

Abu Bishr recited (thumma yajʿalahu) with a fatha on the lam. The author of al-Kamil said: it is weak. End.

(Indeed in that): i.e., in what has been mentioned of sending down rain, bringing out crops by it, and its transitions to the state of debris, (is a reminder): i.e., an admonition and a warning about the wisdom of the One who does this and His power.

﴿Is one whose breast Allah has opened to Islam﴾: it was revealed concerning Hamzah and ʿAli. (Man) is a subject whose predicate is omitted, indicated by ﴿Woe to those whose hearts are hardened﴾; its estimate is: "like the hard-hearted one who turns away from Islam." Abu Lahab and his son were among those whose hearts were hardened. The expression "opening of the breast" is a metaphor for its acceptance of faith, goodness, light and guidance. In a hadith: "How is the opening of the breasts?" He said: "When light enters the heart, it opens and expands." We said: "And what is the sign of that?" He said: "Turning in repentance to the abode of eternity, withdrawing from the abode of delusion, and preparing for death before death."

﴿Woe to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah﴾: i.e., on account of His remembrance; that is, when Allah is mentioned in their presence, their hearts harden. Malik ibn Dinar said: no servant has been struck with a punishment greater than hardness of heart.

(Those) i.e., those whose hearts are hardened, (are in clear error): i.e., in evident confusion, not hidden from one who reflects upon it.

Ibn Ishaq said: The reference is to ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf, Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas, Saʿid ibn Zayd, and al-Zubayr. That is because when Abu Bakr embraced Islam, they heard of it and came to him and said: "Have you become a Muslim?" He said: "Yes," and he reminded them of Allah, so they all believed. Thus it was revealed concerning them, and it is muhkam (definitive in its ruling) for people until the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Taghut: the discussion of it has already passed in al-Baqarah. Al-Hasan recited (al-Tawaghit) in the plural.

﴿That they should not worship it﴾: i.e., its worship. It is a badal al-ishtimal (a substitution of inclusion).

(For them is good tidings): i.e., from Allah, the Exalted, of reward.

(So give good tidings to My servants): they are those who avoid the Taghut and turn to Allah. He placed the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun to indicate that they are indeed those, and so that the descriptive clause follows the apparent noun: ﴿those who listen to the word﴾, which is general over all sayings, ﴿and follow the best of it﴾: a praise of them for the penetration of their insight and their discernment of the best; so when they hear a saying, they examine it.

It was said: the best of speech is the Qur'an and what refers back to it. It was also said: the word is the Qur'an, and its best is what contains pardon, forgiveness, forbearance and the like. Qatadah said: the best of speech is obedience to Allah.

From Ibn ʿAbbas: it is the man who sits with a people, hears a discourse containing both good and bad, and relates the best of what he heard, and refrains from the rest.

(Alladhina) is a description of (ʿibad). It was also said: the pause is at ʿibad, and (alladhina) is a subject whose predicate is (ulaʾika) and what follows it.

﴿Is one against whom the word of punishment has become due﴾: it was said it was revealed concerning Abu Jahl, i.e., the threat of punishment was executed against him. The apparent view is that it is an independent sentence, and (man) is a relative subject whose predicate is omitted. It was said its estimate is: "he grieves over him," and it was said: "he seeks to free himself from him." Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as: "then you deliver him," saying: it is omitted because of the indication of ﴿Would you then rescue﴾ upon it. Al-Zamakhshari also estimated a clause between the hamzah and the fa', so that the hamzah and the fa' each remain in its place, saying: the estimate is: "Are you the master of their affair? Then [is] the one against whom the word of punishment has become due [to be saved]?" This is an opinion in which he stood alone, as far as we know.

What the grammarians say is that the fa' is for coordination, and its place is before the hamzah, but since the hamzah has the right of beginning the sentence, it was placed first; so the original, according to them, is: "fa-man haqqa 'alayhi." On the view that it is an independent sentence, his statement ﴿Would you then rescue those in the Fire?﴾ is a question of reproach, and the pronoun is placed first to indicate that you are not able to rescue him from the Fire; rather no one is able to do that except Allah. A group, among them al-Hawfi and al-Zamakhshari, held that man is conditional, and the answer of the condition is ﴿afa-anta﴾; the fa' is the fa' of the answer which entered upon the clause of the consequence, and the hamzah was repeated to emphasise the meaning of denial and remoteness; and (man fi al-nar), which is apparent, was placed in the position of the pronoun, since the original would be "tunqiduhu"; it was made explicit to publicise their state and to reveal the baseness of their stations. Al-Hawfi said: the interrogative alif was brought when the speech was long, for emphasis; had it not been long, it would not be permissible to bring it, because it is not proper in Arabic to bring the interrogative alif on the noun and another alif on the condition. The meaning of the speech is: "Would you then rescue him?" End.

On this view, an interrogative and a conditional are combined; according to the consensus that the hamzah has been moved forward from what comes after it, the disagreement between Sibawayh and Yunus arises: is the last clause the object of the question, or is it the answer of the condition? On al-Zamakhshari's estimate, the hamzah does not enter upon the conditional noun, so an interrogative and a conditional do not combine; because in his view the interrogative entered upon the omitted clause, which is: "Are you the master of their affair?" and "fa-man" is coordinated to that omitted clause; the conditional clause is coordinated upon the interrogative clause. The deserving of punishment is descended upon them, and they, in this world, are in the position of entering the Fire; and the effort of the Messenger, upon him be peace, in calling them to faith is in the position of rescuing them from the Fire.

When He mentioned the state of the disbelievers in the Fire, and that the losers have canopies of fire above them, He mentioned the state of the believers. The istidrak (contrast) was appropriate here, since it lies between the disbelievers and the believers, so He said: (But those who fear). In that is an exhortation to piety: for them are lofty chambers, above which are built lofty chambers, i.e., the construction of dwellings laid out upon the earth. The pronoun in (from beneath them) refers to both groups, i.e., from beneath the lower chambers and the upper chambers, there being no difference between their highest and lowest. (Promise of Allah) is put in the accusative as a verbal noun emphasising the content of the sentence before it, since it implies the meaning of promise.

(Do you not see): an address and a reproach to the listener, concerning what he should take as a lesson from the acts of Allah which show the passing away and dissolution of this world.

﴿Then He made it flow as springs﴾: i.e., He made it enter channels and fountains. The apparent view is that the water of the springs is from rainwater, which the earth retains and which emerges little by little.

﴿Then He brings out by it crops﴾: He mentions His favour upon us by which our livelihood is sustained.

(Of varying colours): of red, white and yellow; the word "crops" includes all that is sown, both staple and otherwise; or its varieties vary, of wheat, barley, sesame and other things.

(Then it withers): it approaches fruition; (then you see it yellow): i.e., its greenness and freshness have gone.

Abu Bishr recited (thumma yajʿalahu) with a fatha on the lam. The author of al-Kamil said: it is weak. End.

(Indeed in that): i.e., in what has been mentioned of sending down rain, bringing out crops by it, and its transitions to the state of debris, (is a reminder): i.e., an admonition and a warning about the wisdom of the One who does this and His power.

﴿Is one whose breast Allah has opened to Islam﴾: it was revealed concerning Hamzah and ʿAli. (Man) is a subject whose predicate is omitted, indicated by ﴿Woe to those whose hearts are hardened﴾; its estimate is: "like the hard-hearted one who turns away from Islam." Abu Lahab and his son were among those whose hearts were hardened. The expression "opening of the breast" is a metaphor for its acceptance of faith, goodness, light and guidance. In a hadith: "How is the opening of the breasts?" He said: "When light enters the heart, it opens and expands." We said: "And what is the sign of that?" He said: "Turning in repentance to the abode of eternity, withdrawing from the abode of delusion, and preparing for death before death."

﴿Woe to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah﴾: i.e., on account of His remembrance; that is, when Allah is mentioned in their presence, their hearts harden. Malik ibn Dinar said: no servant has been struck with a punishment greater than hardness of heart.

(Those) i.e., those whose hearts are hardened, (are in clear error): i.e., in evident confusion, not hidden from one who reflects upon it.

(p. 423) ﴿Allah has sent down the best of speech, a Book consistent with itself, repeating [its teachings], at which shiver the skins of those who fear their Lord; then their skins and their hearts soften to the remembrance of Allah. That is the guidance of Allah; He guides with it whom He wills, and whoever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide.﴾ ﴿Is one who shields his face from the terrible punishment on the Day of Resurrection [like one who is safe]? It will be said to the wrongdoers: "Taste what you used to earn."﴾ ﴿Those before them denied, and the punishment came upon them from where they did not perceive.﴾ ﴿So Allah made them taste disgrace in the life of this world, but the punishment of the Hereafter is greater, if only they knew.﴾ ﴿And We have certainly presented to the people in this Qur'an every kind of example, that they may be reminded.﴾ ﴿An Arabic Qur'an, free of any crookedness, that they may be mindful of Allah.﴾ ﴿Allah presents an example: a man in whom are partners disputing with one another, and a man belonging wholly to one man. Are the two equal in comparison? All praise is for Allah; but most of them do not know.﴾ ﴿Indeed, you will die, and indeed they will die.﴾ ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord, you will dispute with one another.﴾

It was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that some of the Companions said: "O Messenger of Allah, tell us some good narratives and reports of the ages," so this was revealed: ﴿Allah has sent down the best of speech﴾.

And from Ibn Mas'ud, that the Companions filled Makkah and said to him: "Tell us," so it was revealed.

The beginning with the Name of Allah and the attribution of "sent down" to His pronoun, as a predication upon Him, conveys exaltation of what was sent down and elevation of it, just as you say: "The king honoured so-and-so" is more emphatic than "So-and-so was honoured by the king." The wisdom of this is to begin with the most noble, reminding of what is ascribed to Him, and this is frequent in the Qur'an, such as His saying: ﴿Allah chooses messengers from among the angels﴾ [al-Hajj: 75]. And "a Book" (kitaban) is a substitute (badal) for "the best of speech." Al-Zamakhshari said: "It may also be a circumstantial accusative (hal)." End of quote.

This is based on the premise that "the best of speech" is definite, due to its being annexed to a definite noun. Concerning the superlative (af'al al-tafdil) when annexed to a definite noun, there is a difference of opinion: it is said its annexation is pure (mahdah), and it is said it is not pure.

"Mutashabihan" (consistent) is unrestricted regarding the resemblance of its parts to one another. Its meanings resemble one another, with no contradiction or conflict in them, and its wording is at the utmost eloquence, rhetorical power and harmony, such that it has defeated the great and the eloquent.

The majority read ﴿mathani﴾ with a fatha on the ya'. Hisham, Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bishr read it with a sukun on the ya'. It may be the predicate of an omitted subject, and it may be in the accusative. The ya' was made sukun according to the view of those who make the ya' sukun in all cases, because the letter before it is kasra, to avoid the burden of the vowel on it. ﴿Mathani﴾ appears to be the plural of "mathna," and its meaning: the place of repetition of stories, rulings, beliefs, promise and threat. It is said: it is repeated in the prayer, meaning: recitation and repetition. End of quote.

He described the singular with a plural, because in it there are details, and the details of a thing are its whole. Do you not see that you say: "The Qur'an is suwar and ayat"? Likewise you say: "Rulings and admonitions, repeated." Its original form is "a Book consistent, with chapters, repeated" (mathani), the described noun was omitted and its adjective placed in its stead. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that it be of the type: "a pot of pieces" (burmah a'shar), "a garment of rags" (thawb akhlaq), and that it be a specification (tamyiz) from "mutashabihan," so that it would be transferred from the agent, i.e., "consistent in its repeated parts."

Just as you say: "I saw a man, good in features" (shama'il). The benefit of its being repeated and reiterated is its firm establishment in souls, for they are most averse to hearing admonition and advice.

The apparent meaning is to take the shivering (qasha'rirah) literally, since it is present at fear, perceptible, which a person senses from himself, and it results from the emotional impact. It is said: it is a figurative depiction of the extremity of their fear, and the meaning: when they hear it recited, with its verses of threat, a fear seizes them so that their skins contract.

Then, when they remember Allah and His mercy, their skins soften, i.e., that contraction arising from fear of the hearts departs from them when fear departs from them. "Talin" (soften) was used to imply "tatma'innu" (become at rest): their skins become soft, not contracted, and their hearts hopeful, not fearful; for this reason it takes "ila" (to).

In mentioning the hearts in this clause there is evidence of their being affected upon hearing. So the shivering of the skins sufficed in place of mentioning the fear of the hearts, since the effect stands in place of the cause. When He mentioned softening, He mentioned both. In the mention of softening there is evidence for the omitted element, which is the mercy of Allah, just as in His saying: "When Allah is mentioned, their hearts tremble," the word "trembled" is evidence of the omitted element, i.e., when the threat of Allah and His seizure are mentioned.

Al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib said: The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever's skin shivers from the fear of Allah, his sins fall away from him as leaves fall from a dry tree."

Ibn 'Umar said, when he saw someone fall down from hearing the Qur'an: "Indeed we fear Allah, yet we do not fall down. These people—Satan enters into the bellies of some of them."

Asma' bint Abi Bakr said: The Companions of the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, their eyes would shed tears and their skins would shiver upon hearing the Qur'an. It was said to her: "Indeed, there are people today, when they hear the Qur'an, one of them falls down unconscious." She said: "I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan."

Ibn Sirin said: Between us and those who are struck down upon the recitation of the Qur'an, let one of them be placed against a wall with his legs outstretched, then the whole Qur'an is recited to him; if he throws himself down, then he is truthful.

The reference of "that" (dhalika) is to the Book, or to those two attributes of shivering and softening, i.e., the trace of the guidance of Allah.

﴿Afaman yattaqi﴾ means: "faces" (yastaqbilu), as the poet said:

"The veil fell, and she did not intend to drop it, so she caught it and shielded us with her hand."

Meaning: she faced us with her hand, to shield her face with her hand from being seen.

The apparent meaning of ﴿biwajhihi﴾ is taken literally: since he is cast into the Fire with his hands chained to his feet along with his neck, he has nothing to shield himself from the Fire except his face.

Mujahid said: He is dragged on his face in the Fire. It is also permissible that the face be used to express the whole. It is said: the meaning is a description of the abundance of punishment that reaches them; he shields himself first with his limbs, then it increases until he shields himself with his face, which is the noblest of his limbs; and in it is an answer, and it is the utmost of the punishment.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This meaning, in my view, is more eloquent. In this field goes the saying of the poet:

"He meets the swords with his face and his chest, and makes his head serve as a helmet."

Because he only intended the greatness of his boldness against them; he meets them with every shield, and with everything from himself, even with his face and his chest. End of quote.

"Su'a al-'adhab" means its severest form. The predicate of "man" is omitted; al-Zamakhshari estimated it as: "like one who is secure from punishment," and Ibn 'Atiyyah: "like those who are blessed in Paradise."

﴿And it will be said to the wrongdoers﴾: that is, the keepers of the Fire say this. "Taste what you used to" — that is, the consequence of what you used to "earn" (taksibun) of wicked deeds.

"Those before them denied": an illustration of the Quraysh by the past nations and what their affair came to of destruction.

﴿Then the punishment came upon them from where they did not perceive﴾: from the direction in which they did not realise the punishment would come upon them, and it did not occur to them that evil would come to them from it.

They were in safety, prosperity and joy; then suddenly they were punished, disgraced, humiliated in this world, by being transformed, killed, captured or exiled.

Then He informed that what has been prepared for them in the Hereafter is greater. "An Arabic Qur'an" is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), which is an emphatic circumstance: the real circumstance is "Arabic," and "Qur'an" is a preparatory introduction to it. It is also said: it is in the accusative as praise, and He negated crookedness from it, since it is straight, free of disagreement and contradiction.

'Uthman ibn 'Affan said: "not disordered." Ibn 'Abbas said: "not in disagreement." Mujahid said: "not ambiguous." al-Suddi said: "not created." It is said: "not ungrammatical."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say: why was it not said 'upright' or 'not crooked'?" I say: there are two benefits in it. One: negating that there is any crookedness in it at all, as He said: ﴿and has not made for Him any crookedness﴾ [al-Kahf: 1]. The second: that the word "'iwaj" (crookedness) is specific to meanings, not to physical objects. It is also said: the intended meaning of "'iwaj" is doubt and ambiguity, and he recited:

"There has come to you with certainty, free of any crookedness, from God, a word that is not false." End of quote.

When He mentioned that He has presented in the Qur'an "every kind of example" — that is, of what is needed — He presented here an example for one who worships many gods and one who worships Allah alone. He illustrated it with a man owned by several owners of bad character; he cannot satisfy each one of them in his purpose, since they do not accommodate one another due to their contention, and each of them demands that he fulfil his need completely; so he is always in toil, fatigue and blame from each of them.

And another man, wholly owned by one man: he is occupied with his service and nothing distracts him from it; his master is pleased with him if he has devoted himself to his service and exerted his effort in fulfilling his needs, so he receives nothing from his master but kindness. The discussion of the accusative of "example" has already been mentioned, and what follows it.

Al-Kisa'i said: "rajulan" is in the accusative by dropping the preposition, meaning: an example for a man, or "in a man, in it," meaning: in his servitude, shared; and "fihi" is connected to "shuraka'" (partners). 'Abd Allah, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Zuhri and al-Hasan (with a variant from him) read "saliman" as an active participle from "salima," meaning: pure from partnership. Al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shaybah, Abu Raja', Talhah and al-Hasan (with a variant from him), and the rest of the seven, read "salaman" with a fatha on the sin and the lam.

Ibn Jubayr read "silman" with a kasra on the sin and a sukun on the lam; both are verbal nouns if described by them, as an intensification of purity from partnership. It has also been read: "wa rajulun (p. 425) salimun" with both in the nominative. Al-Zamakhshari said: meaning, "and there is a man, pure, for a man." End of quote, so he made the predicate there.

It is permissible that "wa rajulun" be a subject (mubtada'), because it is a place of detail, since what indicates it has already been mentioned, so it is like the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"When she weeps from behind her, she turns to him with one side, and with the other side, to us, unchanged."

Al-Zamakhshari said: He made him a man only so that he would be more perceptive regarding what he would be unhappy or happy about, for a woman and a child may be unaware of that.

"Mathalan" is in the accusative as a specification transferred from the agent, since the estimate is: "Is their example equal?" He limited the specification to the singular, because it is what is limited to at first in His saying: "Allah struck an example," and to clarify the kind. It was also read: "mathalayni" (two examples), which agrees with the state of the two men.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is permissible, for the one who reads "mathalayni," that the pronoun in "yastawiyan" (are they equal) refers to the two examples, because the estimate is "the example of a man," and the meaning: "Are they equal in what returns to description?" as one says: "Two men are sufficient for them." End of quote.

The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in "yastawiyan" refers to the two men. But if you make it refer to the two examples, which he mentioned, that the estimate is "the example of a man and a man," then the specification in that case would have been understood from the specified noun, which is the pronoun, since the estimate becomes: "Are the two examples equal as two examples?"

Say: "All praise is for Allah": that is, the praise and commendation are for Allah and not for other than Him, and He is the One whose oneness is established, so He is the One who must be praised. "But most of them do not know," so they associate others with Him.

The expression "All praise is for Allah" implies the destruction of them, through His saying: ﴿So the root of the people who did wrong was cut off, and all praise is for Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-An'am: 45].

When they did not turn to these manifest proofs, He informed everyone that they are dying and will return to Him, and that your disputing will be before Him on the Day of Resurrection, and He is the Just Judge, so the truthful is distinguished from the falsifier. He, peace be upon him, and his followers are the truthful, the victorious, who are successful with triumph and dominance, and the disbelievers are the falsifiers.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 39, verses 23–31 (part 2 of 2):

The pronoun in (wa-innaka) is addressed to the Messenger, and his community is included with him in this. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in (wa-innahum) refers to the disbelievers. The second-person pronoun in (innaka) took precedence over the third-person pronoun in (innahum), and for this reason ﴿takhtasimun﴾ came in the second person, meaning that you will argue against them, [since] you have indeed conveyed [the message] and they denied it, and you exerted yourself in the call while they persisted in obstinacy.

Abu al-'Aliyah said: "They are the people of the qibla (Muslims), who will dispute among themselves on the Day of Resurrection concerning their injustices."

The one who went furthest astray is he who held that this dispute is caused by what took place over the killing of Uthman and what occurred between Ali and Mu'awiyah because of that, may Allah be pleased with them.

It has also been said: everyone will dispute. The disbelievers will dispute with one another until it is said to them: "Do not dispute before Me." The believers will confront the disbelievers with proofs, and the people of the qibla will have disputes among themselves.

Ibn al-Zubayr, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Ibn Muhaysin, 'Isa, al-Yamani, Ibn Abi Ghawth, and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read: (innaka ma'itun wa-innahum ma'itun), and this conveys the occurrence of the attribute; whereas the majority read: (mayyitun wa-mayyitun), which conveys permanence and necessity, like "alive" (hayy).

When they did not turn to these manifest proofs, He informed everyone that they are dying and will return to Him, and that your disputing will be before Him on the Day of Resurrection, and He is the Just Judge, so the truthful is distinguished from the falsifier. He, peace be upon him, and his followers are the truthful, the victorious, who are successful with triumph and dominance, and the disbelievers are the falsifiers.
