**Qur'an 39:56–63:**

﴿Lest a soul should say: "Alas for me, for what I neglected concerning Allah, and indeed I was among those who mocked."﴾ ﴿Or lest it say: "If only Allah had guided me, I would have been among the righteous."﴾ ﴿Or lest it say, when it sees the punishment: "If only I had a return, so that I might be among the good-doers."﴾ ﴿Yes, indeed, My signs came to you, but you denied them, grew arrogant, and were among the disbelievers.﴾ ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection you will see those who lied against Allah with their faces blackened. Is there not in Hell an abode for the arrogant?﴾ ﴿And Allah will deliver those who were mindful of Him by their salvation; no evil will touch them, nor will they grieve.﴾ ﴿Allah is the Creator of all things, and He is Guardian over all things.﴾ ﴿To Him belong the keys of the heavens and the earth. And those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah, they are the losers.﴾

It has been narrated that among the Children of Israel there was a scholar who abandoned his knowledge and became dissolute. Iblis came to him and said: "Enjoy the world, then repent." He obeyed him and spent his wealth in sinfulness. Then the Angel of Death came to him at the most pleasurable time he had known, and he said: ﴿Alas for me, for what I neglected concerning Allah﴾, and his life had gone in obedience to Satan, and he had angered his Lord. He regretted it at a time when regret would not benefit him, so Allah revealed his report.

﴿Lest a soul should say﴾: it is a *maf'ul li-ajlihi* (object of purpose, an accusative noun indicating the reason for an action). Ibn 'Atiyya therefore supposed it to mean: "Turn in repentance lest a soul should say."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "out of dislike that a soul should say." Al-Hawfi said: "We warned you for fear that a soul should say." The word *nafs* (soul) is indefinite because either some souls are intended, namely the soul of the disbeliever, or a great number is intended, as al-A'sha said:

*"And many a generous helper, if I called out to him, came to me, shaking his head in anger."*

He means groups of noble men who would help him, not a single noble man. Or the intended meaning is a soul distinguished from other souls by its extreme wickedness in disbelief, or by a great punishment.

Al-Zamakhshari mentioned these possibilities, but the apparent meaning is the first. Al-Jumhur read ﴿Alas for me﴾ (*ya hasrata*) with the *ya* of the first person replaced by an *alif*. Abu Ja'far read *ya hasrata* with the *ya* of the first person (*ya al-idafa*). And it is narrated from him as *ya hasrati* with both *alif* and *ya*, combining the substitute and the substituted, the *ya* being either fatha-vowelled or sukun-vowelled.

Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said in his work *Kitab al-Lawami'*: "If one goes to the view that he intended the dual of *hasrah* (regret), like *labbayka* and *sa'dayka*, because their meaning is 'devotion after devotion' and 'happiness after happiness', then likewise this regret is 'regret after regret', because of the abundance of their regrets on that day. Or if he intended only two regrets, from the food of Paradise for entering the Fire, that would be a valid position, and the *alif* of the dual would be in the estimation of a *ya*, according to the dialect of Balharith ibn Ka'b." End of quotation.

Ibn Kathir read in pause *ya hasrataahu* with the *ha* of pausal silence (*ha' al-sakt*). Sibawayh said: "The meaning of calling out to regret and woe is: 'This is your time, so come forth.'"

*Al-janb* means the side, and it is impossible for Allah to have a body part, so attributing *janb* to Him is figurative. Mujahid and al-Suddi said: "in the matter of Allah." Al-Dahhak said: "in His remembrance," meaning the Qur'an and acting upon it. It was also said: "in the direction of His obedience." *Al-janb* means direction, and a poet said:

*"Concerning a side that is called, she cut me off with reproach, but Sulaymá's reproach was praise."*

And a rajaz poet said:

*"The people are a side, and the commander is a side."*

It is said: "I am at the side and flank and vicinity of so-and-so," and "so-and-so is soft of side and flank." Then they said: "He neglected his side," meaning his right. Sabiq al-Barbari said:

*"Will you not fear Allah concerning a lover whose liver is burning with longing for you and is torn apart?"*

This is from the figure of speech (*kinaya*), because when you place a matter in a man's location and place, you have ascribed it to him. Do you not see his saying:

*"Indeed generosity, nobility and bounty are in a tent pitched over the son of al-Hashraj."*

From this is the people's saying: "For your sake I did such and such," meaning "for your benefit," and "I did this on your behalf."

The *ma* in ﴿what I neglected﴾ is verbal-masdarial (*masdariyya*), meaning: "for my neglect in obedience to Allah."

﴿And indeed I was among those who mocked﴾. Qatada said: "It was not enough for him that he wasted obedience to Allah until he mocked its people." Al-Zamakhshari said: "The position of *wa-in kuntu* (and indeed I was) is in the accusative as a *hal* (circumstantial clause), as if he said: 'I neglected while I was mocking,' that is, I neglected in the state of my mockery." End of quotation.

It appears that it is a resumptive statement (*isti'naf*) informing about himself regarding what he was upon in the world, not a circumstantial clause.

﴿Or lest it say: "If only Allah had guided me"﴾, that is: He created guidance in me by compulsion, which is outside wisdom; or by grace (*lutf*), but I was not among its people so that I would be given grace; or by revelation, and indeed it came, but he turned away and did not follow it until he would be guided. He says this only out of bewilderment regarding his matter and as an excuse with what would benefit him, just as He related their excuse by the misguidance of the leaders and the devils. [p. 436] Similar to it: "If Allah had guided us, we would have guided you." End of quotation. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazila.

﴿Fa-akuna﴾ is in the accusative as a reply to the wish indicated by *law* (if only), or as an object of *karra* (return), since it is a verbal noun (*masdar*), so it is like His saying:

*"Of it there is nothing for you except remembrance and regret, and you ask about its riders, where they have set their course."*

And the other's saying:

*"The wearing of a cloak and my eye being comforted are dearer to me than the wearing of fine silks."*

The difference between the two is that when the *fa* is in reply to a wish, *anna* (that) must be implied; and the being is then consequent upon the realization of the wish, not itself a wish. But when it is for coordination with *karra*, both the explicit and implicit *anna* are permissible, and the being is itself wished for.

*Bala* (yes, indeed) is a particle of answer to a negation, or to a question that has the interrogative *hamza* of affirmation. Since His saying ﴿if Allah had guided me﴾ and its answer implies a negation of guidance, as if he had said: "Allah did not guide me," it was said to him: ﴿Yes, indeed, My signs came to you, guiding you﴾, but you denied them. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is a rejection from Allah against him, and its meaning is: 'Yes, indeed, you were guided by revelation.'" End of quotation, following the rules of the Mu'tazila.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The right use of *bala* is that it comes after a negation, and it is a confirmation. His saying *bala* is an answer to an implied negation, as if the soul had said: 'My life in the world did not have room for consideration,' or said: 'For me the matter was not made clear in the world,' and similar." End of quotation.

But the right use of *bala* is not what was mentioned; rather its right use is to be an answer to a negation. Then the affirmation was treated as a negation, and for this reason some Arabs did not treat it this way, and answered it with *na'am* (yes). This also occurred in the speech of Sibawayh himself, that he answered the affirmation with *na'am*, following some Arabs.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: why did He not combine the answer with that to which it is an answer, namely His saying ﴿if Allah had guided me﴾, and not separate them by a verse?" I say: because it could not be otherwise: either it would be placed before the other of the three contexts, thus separating them, or the middle context would be delayed. The first was not good because of what it contains of disrupting the composition by joining the contexts together. As for the second, it contains the breaking of order, which is regret over neglect in obedience, then the excuse of lacking guidance, then the wish for a return. So the correct arrangement was what came, namely that He related the soul's statements in their order and arrangement, then answered from among them what required an answer." End of quotation, and it is a fine statement.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿قد جاءتك﴾ (*qad jā'atka*) with a fatha on the *kaf* and a fatha on the *ta'* following it, addressing the disbelieving person (*dhu al-nafs*). Ibn Ya'mar, al-Jahdari, Abu Haywa, al-Za'farani, Ibn Miqsam, Mas'ud ibn Salih, al-Shafi'i from Ibn Kathir, Muhammad ibn 'Isa in his selection, and from Nusayr and al-'Absi read it with a kasra on the *kaf* and the *ta'*, addressing the soul. This is the reading of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq and his daughter 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with them both, and Umm Salama narrated both from the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Hasan, al-A'raj and al-A'mash read *ji'tuka* with a *hamza* without a madd, in the pattern of *bi'tuka*, and it is metathesized from *jā'atka*: the last radical was moved forward and the middle radical moved back, so the *alif* dropped, as it dropped in *ramat* and *'arat*.

When He mentioned the speech of the disbeliever, He mentioned what befalls him on the Day of Resurrection of warning about the evil of his end, and implicitly a threat to his contemporaries, upon him be peace.

The seeing here is seeing by sight. Their lying is their attributing to Him, exalted is He, daughters, a consort and a son, and their legislating what Allah did not permit.

The apparent meaning is that it is general to those who lie against Allah, and some restricted it to the polytheist Arabs and the People of the Two Books. Al-Hasan said: "They are the Qadariyya, who say: 'If we will, we do, and if we will, we do not do.'"

The judge (al-Qadi) said: "It is necessary to apply the verse to all of the Mujbira (predestinarians who deny human agency), the Mushabbiha (anthropomorphists), and everyone who describes Allah with what is not fitting for Him, by negation and by affirmation. He has ascribed to Him what should not be ascribed to Him, so all of them lied against Allah. Therefore restricting the verse to the Mujbira and the Mushabbiha and the Jews and Christians is not permissible."

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿they lied against Allah﴾: they described Him with what is not permissible for Him, and He is exalted above it. They ascribed to Him a son and a partner, and they said: ﴿These are our intercessors with Allah﴾ [Yunus 10:18], and they said: ﴿If the Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them﴾ [al-Zukhruf 43:20], and they said: ﴿And Allah has commanded us to do it﴾ [al-A'raf 7:28]. And there is no distance between them and a people who ascribe folly to Him by committing ugly deeds. And it is possible that He creates a creation without purpose, and His saying "without purpose" [is a statement of this view]; and they wrong Him by charging Him with what cannot be borne; and they make Him corporeal by making Him visible, perceptible by the senses; and they affirm for Him a hand and a foot and a side, hidden behind the *balkafa* (a particular cloth covering); and they make for Him equals by their affirming a foot alongside Him. End of quotation.

The speech of the one before him follows the manner of the Mu'tazila. The apparent meaning is that the seeing is seeing by sight, and that ﴿their faces blackened﴾ is a clause in the position of a circumstantial state (*hal*). In it there is a rejection of al-Zamakhshari, who claimed that the deletion of the *waw* from a nominal clause in the position of the second object is possible; and this is far-fetched, because the sight's connection to the perception of bodies and their colours is more apparent than the heart's connection.

It is also read: *wujuhahum musawwadatan* with both accusative, so *wujuhuhum* is a partial substitute (*badal ba'd min kull*) from the whole. Ubayy read *ujuhuhum* with the *waw* replaced by a *hamza*. The apparent meaning is that the blackening is literal, as already mentioned in His saying ﴿As for those whose faces turned black﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:106]. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is possible that there is figurative expression in the phrase, and that blackness is used to express the dejection of their faces, the predominance of their concern, and the evident sorrow."

When the Exalted mentioned the state of those who lie against Allah, He mentioned the state of those who are mindful, that is, [those who avoid] lying against Allah and other than Him, which leads its doer to the blackening of his face. In this is encouragement toward this sublime attribute, which is mindfulness (*taqwa*). Al-Suddi said: ﴿by their salvation﴾: by their success. It is said: "He succeeded by such and such," if he prospered by it and achieved his aim. The explanation of *mafaza* (salvation) is His saying: ﴿no evil will touch them, nor will they grieve﴾, as if it was said: "What is their salvation?" It was answered: "No evil will touch them," meaning He delivers them by negating evil and grief from them. Or it is by means of what saves them, from His saying: ﴿So do not think them to be secure from the punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:188], that is, in a place of deliverance from it, because deliverance is among the greatest success, and the cause of their deliverance is righteous deeds. For this reason Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, explained *mafaza* as good deeds. It is also permissible that it refers to the cause of their success, because righteous deeds are the cause of success, which is entry into Paradise.

It is also permissible for righteous deeds themselves to be called *mafaza*, because they are its cause.

(If you ask): what is the grammatical position (*i'rab*) of ﴿no evil will touch them﴾ according to the two explanations? (I say): as for the first explanation, it has no position, because it is a resumed statement; and as for the second, its position is accusative as a circumstantial state. End of quotation.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿by their salvation﴾ in the singular, while al-Sulami, al-Hasan, al-A'raj, al-A'mash, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr read it in the plural, because deliverance has types and the causes are different.

Abu 'Ali said: masdars are pluralized when their kinds differ, as in His saying: ﴿and you assume about Allah assumptions﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:10]. Al-Farra' said: both readings are correct; you say: "The affair of people has become clear" and "the affairs of people." 

When the Exalted mentioned the promise and the threat, He returned to the proofs of divinity and monotheism, mentioning that He is the Creator of all things, which indicates the deeds of the servants, since they are included in the generality of "all things." And that He is over all things, standing to preserve them and direct them.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 39, verses 56–63 (part 2 of 2):

﴿To Him belong the keys (maqalid) of the heavens and the earth﴾: Ibn ʿAbbās said: "keys (maftīḥ)." This is a metaphor, as you say: "The key (miftāḥ) to this matter is in the hand of so-and-so."

And from the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "The maqalid are: there is no god but God, God is greatest, glory be to God, praise be to God, and there is no power nor strength except with God, the Most High, the Mighty. He is the First and the Last, the Manifest and the Hidden. In His hand is the good. He gives life and causes death, and He is over all things capable."

Its interpretation according to this is that God has these words, by which He is declared one and glorified, and they are the keys to the good of the heavens and the earth. Whoever among the God-fearing speaks them attains (the good).

﴿And those who disbelieve in the signs of God﴾, meaning His words of tawhid and glorification, ﴿those are the losers﴾.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: "(If you ask): with what is the statement 'And those who disbelieve' connected? (I answer): with His statement, ﴿God will deliver those who were mindful of Him through their salvation﴾, and ('those who disbelieve') ﴿are the losers﴾." He placed between them (an interjection): that the Creator of all things, who has dominion over them, nothing of the deeds of the accountable is hidden from Him, nor what they deserve of recompense for them, and that ﴿To Him belong the keys of the heavens and the earth﴾.

Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Rāzī said: "This, in my view, is weak for two reasons. The first: the occurrence of a large intervening element between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined is remote. The second: God's statement, ﴿God will deliver those who were mindful of Him﴾, is a verbal sentence (jumla fiʿliyya), and His statement, ﴿And those who disbelieve﴾, is a nominal sentence (jumla ismiyya), and conjoining a nominal sentence to a verbal sentence is not permitted. The closer view, in my opinion, is to say: when He was described with the attributes of divinity and majesty, namely that He is the Creator of all things and that He possesses the keys of the heavens and the earth, He said: those who disbelieve in these manifest and dazzling signs are the losers." End of quote. This is not a large intervening element. As for his statement that conjoining a nominal sentence to a verbal sentence is not permitted, it is the speech of one who has not reflected on the language of the Arabs nor examined the chapter on the ishtighāl construction (bāb al-ishtighāl, the construction in which a verb is suppressed and its object is referred to by a pronoun).

As for his statement, "the closer view in my opinion," it is taken from the words of al-Zamakhsharī, and it has been connected to what follows it, on the basis that everything in the heavens and the earth has God as its Creator and the One who opens its door. ﴿And those who disbelieve﴾ and deny that the matter is so, ﴿those are the losers﴾.

The seeing here is seeing by sight. Their lying is their attributing to Him, exalted is He, daughters, a consort and a son, and their legislating what Allah did not permit.

The apparent meaning is that it is general to those who lie against Allah, and some restricted it to the polytheist Arabs and the People of the Two Books. Al-Hasan said: "They are the Qadariyya, who say: 'If we will, we do, and if we will, we do not do.'"

The judge (al-Qadi) said: "It is necessary to apply the verse to all of the Mujbira (predestinarians who deny human agency), the Mushabbiha (anthropomorphists), and everyone who describes Allah with what is not fitting for Him, by negation and by affirmation. He has ascribed to Him what should not be ascribed to Him, so all of them lied against Allah. Therefore restricting the verse to the Mujbira and the Mushabbiha and the Jews and Christians is not permissible."

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿they lied against Allah﴾: they described Him with what is not permissible for Him, and He is exalted above it. They ascribed to Him a son and a partner, and they said: ﴿These are our intercessors with Allah﴾ [Yunus 10:18], and they said: ﴿If the Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them﴾ [al-Zukhruf 43:20], and they said: ﴿And Allah has commanded us to do it﴾ [al-A'raf 7:28]. And there is no distance between them and a people who ascribe folly to Him by committing ugly deeds. And it is possible that He creates a creation without purpose, and His saying "without purpose" [is a statement of this view]; and they wrong Him by charging Him with what cannot be borne; and they make Him corporeal by making Him visible, perceptible by the senses; and they affirm for Him a hand and a foot and a side, hidden behind the *balkafa* (a particular cloth covering); and they make for Him equals by their affirming a foot alongside Him. End of quotation.

The speech of the one before him follows the manner of the Mu'tazila. The apparent meaning is that the seeing is seeing by sight, and that ﴿their faces blackened﴾ is a clause in the position of a circumstantial state (*hal*). In it there is a rejection of al-Zamakhshari, who claimed that the deletion of the *waw* from a nominal clause in the position of the second object is possible; and this is far-fetched, because the sight's connection to the perception of bodies and their colours is more apparent than the heart's connection.

It is also read: *wujuhahum musawwadatan* with both accusative, so *wujuhuhum* is a partial substitute (*badal ba'd min kull*) from the whole. Ubayy read *ujuhuhum* with the *waw* replaced by a *hamza*. The apparent meaning is that the blackening is literal, as already mentioned in His saying ﴿As for those whose faces turned black﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:106]. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is possible that there is figurative expression in the phrase, and that blackness is used to express the dejection of their faces, the predominance of their concern, and the evident sorrow."

When the Exalted mentioned the state of those who lie against Allah, He mentioned the state of those who are mindful, that is, [those who avoid] lying against Allah and other than Him, which leads its doer to the blackening of his face. In this is encouragement toward this sublime attribute, which is mindfulness (*taqwa*). Al-Suddi said: ﴿by their salvation﴾: by their success. It is said: "He succeeded by such and such," if he prospered by it and achieved his aim. The explanation of *mafaza* (salvation) is His saying: ﴿no evil will touch them, nor will they grieve﴾, as if it was said: "What is their salvation?" It was answered: "No evil will touch them," meaning He delivers them by negating evil and grief from them. Or it is by means of what saves them, from His saying: ﴿So do not think them to be secure from the punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:188], that is, in a place of deliverance from it, because deliverance is among the greatest success, and the cause of their deliverance is righteous deeds. For this reason Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, explained *mafaza* as good deeds. It is also permissible that it refers to the cause of their success, because righteous deeds are the cause of success, which is entry into Paradise.

It is also permissible for righteous deeds themselves to be called *mafaza*, because they are its cause.

(If you ask): what is the grammatical position (*i'rab*) of ﴿no evil will touch them﴾ according to the two explanations? (I say): as for the first explanation, it has no position, because it is a resumed statement; and as for the second, its position is accusative as a circumstantial state. End of quotation.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿by their salvation﴾ in the singular, while al-Sulami, al-Hasan, al-A'raj, al-A'mash, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr read it in the plural, because deliverance has types and the causes are different.

Abu 'Ali said: masdars are pluralized when their kinds differ, as in His saying: ﴿and you assume about Allah assumptions﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:10]. Al-Farra' said: both readings are correct; you say: "The affair of people has become clear" and "the affairs of people." 

When the Exalted mentioned the promise and the threat, He returned to the proofs of divinity and monotheism, mentioning that He is the Creator of all things, which indicates the deeds of the servants, since they are included in the generality of "all things." And that He is over all things, standing to preserve them and direct them.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 39, verses 56–63 (part 2 of 2):

﴿To Him belong the keys (maqalid) of the heavens and the earth﴾: Ibn ʿAbbās said: "keys (maftīḥ)." This is a metaphor, as you say: "The key (miftāḥ) to this matter is in the hand of so-and-so."

And from the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "The maqalid are: there is no god but God, God is greatest, glory be to God, praise be to God, and there is no power nor strength except with God, the Most High, the Mighty. He is the First and the Last, the Manifest and the Hidden. In His hand is the good. He gives life and causes death, and He is over all things capable."

Its interpretation according to this is that God has these words, by which He is declared one and glorified, and they are the keys to the good of the heavens and the earth. Whoever among the God-fearing speaks them attains (the good).

﴿And those who disbelieve in the signs of God﴾, meaning His words of tawhid and glorification, ﴿those are the losers﴾.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: "(If you ask): with what is the statement 'And those who disbelieve' connected? (I answer): with His statement, ﴿God will deliver those who were mindful of Him through their salvation﴾, and ('those who disbelieve') ﴿are the losers﴾." He placed between them (an interjection): that the Creator of all things, who has dominion over them, nothing of the deeds of the accountable is hidden from Him, nor what they deserve of recompense for them, and that ﴿To Him belong the keys of the heavens and the earth﴾.

Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Rāzī said: "This, in my view, is weak for two reasons. The first: the occurrence of a large intervening element between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined is remote. The second: God's statement, ﴿God will deliver those who were mindful of Him﴾, is a verbal sentence (jumla fiʿliyya), and His statement, ﴿And those who disbelieve﴾, is a nominal sentence (jumla ismiyya), and conjoining a nominal sentence to a verbal sentence is not permitted. The closer view, in my opinion, is to say: when He was described with the attributes of divinity and majesty, namely that He is the Creator of all things and that He possesses the keys of the heavens and the earth, He said: those who disbelieve in these manifest and dazzling signs are the losers." End of quote. This is not a large intervening element. As for his statement that conjoining a nominal sentence to a verbal sentence is not permitted, it is the speech of one who has not reflected on the language of the Arabs nor examined the chapter on the ishtighāl construction (bāb al-ishtighāl, the construction in which a verb is suppressed and its object is referred to by a pronoun).

As for his statement, "the closer view in my opinion," it is taken from the words of al-Zamakhsharī, and it has been connected to what follows it, on the basis that everything in the heavens and the earth has God as its Creator and the One who opens its door. ﴿And those who disbelieve﴾ and deny that the matter is so, ﴿those are the losers﴾.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 39, verses 64–70 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Say, "Do you order me to worship other than God, you ignorant ones?"﴾ ﴿And it has been revealed to you and to those before you: "If you associate partners with God, your deeds will surely be nullified, and you will surely be among the losers."﴾ ﴿Rather, worship God alone, and be among the thankful.﴾ ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure, while the earth entirely will be His handful on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens will be folded up in His right hand. Glory be to Him, exalted above what they associate with Him.﴾ ﴿And the Trumpet will be blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will swoon, except whom God wills. Then it will be blown again, and behold, they will be standing, looking on.﴾ ﴿And the earth will shine with the light of its Lord, the Book will be placed, the prophets and the witnesses will be brought, and judgment will be passed between them with truth, and they will not be wronged.﴾ ﴿And every soul will be paid in full for what it did, and He is most knowing of what they do.﴾

It is narrated that the polytheists said to the Messenger (peace be upon him): "Touch some of our gods, and we will believe in your God." The word *ghayra* (other than) is in the accusative, governed by *a'budu* (I worship).

Al-Akhfash said: *ta'murunni* is cancelled (*mulgha*, i.e., has no grammatical effect). He also said: *afa-ghayra* is in the accusative governed by *ta'murunni*, not by *a'budu*, because the relative clause (*al-sila*) does not govern what precedes it, since the relative pronoun (*al-mawsul*) has been deleted and the noun has taken the nominative, as in the line of poetry:

"Ah, you who restrain me from entering the battle,"

The relative clause together with the relative pronoun is in the accusative position as a substitute (*badal*) for it. That is: "Do you order me to worship other than God?" Its meaning: "Do you order me to worship other than God?"

Al-Zamakhshari said: Or it is governed by what the sentence *ta'murunni a'budu* implies, because it means: "You worship and say to me, 'I worship it,' and 'Do you say to me that I worship other than God?' Likewise, 'Do you order me to worship other than God?' Do you order me that I worship?" The evidence for the soundness of this view is the reading of those who read *a'buda* with the accusative, meaning with a *fatha* on the *dal*, by implying *an* (that). The majority read *ta'murunni* with the *nun* assimilated into the *nun of protection* (*nun al-wiqaya*), with the *ya'* quiescent. Ibn Kathir read it with a *fatha* on the *ya'*.

Ibn Amir read *ta'murunnani* with two *nun*s, according to the original form. Nafi' read *ta'muruni* with a single *nun* that is kasra-d and a *fatha* on the *ya'*. Ibn Atiyyah said: This is by deleting the single *nun*, which is the one that prepares for the *ya'* of the speaker. The first *nun* may not be deleted; that would be a grammatical error (*lahn*), because it is the sign of the nominative of the verb. End of quotation.

There is disagreement on this matter. Some say the deleted one is the *nun* of nominative case (*nun al-raf'*), and some say it is the *nun* of protection. It is not an error, because the construction is agreed upon, and the disagreement concerns which of the two was deleted. We choose that it is the *nun* of the nominative.

Since the command to worship other than God proceeds only from a foolish ignorant person, He addressed them with the description that requires this, saying: ﴿you ignorant ones﴾.

Since association with God is impossible for one whom God has protected, the phrase ﴿if you associate partners﴾ must be interpreted as addressed to the hearer, and the address continues on this interpretation. What supports this interpretation is that the singular address in ﴿if you associate partners﴾ is not a direct return of the address to the Messenger, for if he were the one addressed, the construction would be *la'in ashraktuma* (if you two associate partners), so that the pronoun would include those before him, and the address would be given precedence.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, "The ones referred to are a group, so how does He say ﴿if you associate partners﴾ in the singular?" I say: its meaning is: "If it is revealed to you, if you associate partners, your deed will be nullified, and to those before you likewise, and it is revealed to you and to each one of them ﴿if you associate partners﴾," as you say, "He clothed us with a garment," meaning each one of us. If you say, "How is this statement valid, given God's knowledge that His messengers do not associate partners and their deeds are not nullified?" I say: it is on the basis of supposition and impossibilities, whose supposition is valid. Then he mentioned words that are to be considered in his book. End of quotation.

This verse is used as evidence that the deeds of an apostate, including prayer and other acts, are nullified. ﴿Was revealed﴾ (*uhiya*) is in the passive voice. It appears that the revelation is these sentences from His words ﴿if you associate partners﴾ up to ﴿among the losers﴾. This is not permissible according to the school of the Basrans, because sentences cannot function as the subject, so they cannot stand in place of the subject.

Muqatil said: It was revealed to you concerning monotheism (*bi-l-tawhid*), and monotheism is omitted. Then he said: ﴿If you associate partners, your deeds will surely be nullified﴾, and the address is to the Prophet (peace be upon him) specifically. End of quotation.

So what stands in place of the subject is the prepositional phrase, which is *ilayka* (to you), and *bi-l-tawhid* is an optional element (*fadla*) whose deletion is permissible because what precedes it indicates it.

The majority read ﴿will surely be nullified﴾ in the active voice, with ﴿your deed﴾ as its subject, in the nominative. It was also read as *layuhbitanna* with a *ya'*, from *ahbata* (to nullify), with *'amalahu* in the accusative, meaning: God will surely nullify your deed, or association will nullify your deed. It was also read with a *nun*, that is *lanuhbitanna 'amalaka* with the accusative, and the divine name is in the accusative governed by ﴿worship﴾ (*fa-'bud*) according to the pattern of their saying: "Zayd, so strike him." It has a full treatment in grammar, and how this *fa'* entered.

Al-Farra' said: If you wish, its accusative can be by a verb hidden before it, as if it were estimated: "Worship God, so worship Him."

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿Rather, worship God alone﴾, as a response to what they ordered him to do of touching some of their gods, as if he said: "Do not worship what they order you to worship. Rather, if you are wise, worship God." So the condition was deleted, and the advancing of the object was made a substitute for it. End of quotation.

The advancing of the object cannot be a substitute for the condition, because it is permissible to say: "Zayd, then Amr, strike," so if it were a substitute, it would not be permissible to combine both.

﴿And be among the thankful﴾, for His blessings, the greatest of which is guidance to the religion of God. ʿIsa read *Bal Allahu* (with *Allahu* in the nominative), while the majority read it in the accusative.

﴿They did not measure God with His true measure﴾, meaning they did not know Him with true knowledge, and they did not estimate Him in themselves with His true estimation, since they associated others with Him and equated Him with stone and wood in worship.

Al-A'mash read ﴿with His true measure﴾ with a *fatha* on the *dal*. Al-Hasan, ʿIsa, Abu Nawfal and Abu Haywah read ﴿they did not measure﴾ with a shadda on the *dal*, and ﴿with His true measure﴾ with a *fatha* on the *dal*, meaning: they did not truly magnify Him. The pronoun in ﴿they measured﴾ — Ibn ʿAbbas said: it refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh. This whole verse was a discourse addressed to them and a refutation of them. It was also said that it was revealed concerning a group of Jews who spoke about the attributes of God and His majesty, so they denied and anthropomorphized Him and brought every kind of confusion. This sentence is mentioned in al-Anʿam, in al-Hajj, and here.

When He informed them that they had not known Him with true knowledge, He alerted them to His greatness and the sublimity of His station, by way of depiction and imagination, saying: ﴿while the earth entirely will be His handful on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens will be folded up in His right hand﴾.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The purpose of this statement, when taken as it is in its whole and collectively, is to depict His greatness and to bring attention to the reality of His majesty only, without taking the handful or the right hand toward a literal direction or a figurative direction. End of quotation.

He means: "or a specific figurative direction." The informing is depiction, and imagination is from figurative language. Others said: The basic principle in speech is to take it on its literal meaning. If a separate proof establishes the impossibility of taking it literally, then it must be turned to figurative meaning.

So the words "handful" and "right hand" are literal in reference to the organ, but the rational proof stands on the impossibility of attributing organs and limbs to God the Exalted. Therefore it is necessary to take it as figurative. That is because one says: "So-and-so is in the handful of so-and-so," when he is under his management and control, and from it comes ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾ [al-Muʾminun: 6], where the meaning is that it is owned by them. "This house is in the hand of so-and-so," and "so-and-so took such-and-such and it came into his handful," meaning his sole possession of it. All of this is widespread figurative usage in common use.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: Here the right hand and the handful are an expression for power, and whatever comes to mind in the breast other than this is false.

What al-Qadi (meaning Ibn al-Tayyib) held, that they are attributes additional to the essential attributes, is a weak view, and according to what comes to mind in souls which knowledge has not encompassed.

He said, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Glory be to Him, exalted above what they associate with Him﴾, meaning: He is free from all the doubts that do not befit Him. End of quotation.

Al-Qaffal said: This is like the saying of one who says: "He did not estimate me with my true estimation, and I am the one who did such-and-such," meaning: since you know that my condition and attribute are this which I have mentioned, it is necessary that you not err concerning my rank and station. Its parallel is: ﴿How can you disbelieve in God when you were dead and He gave you life?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 28], meaning: how can you disbelieve in One whose attribute and dominion are this? So likewise here: ﴿they did not measure God with His true measure﴾, meaning: they claimed that He has partners, and that He cannot give life to the dead, though the earth and the heavens are in the handful of His power. End of quotation.

﴿And the earth﴾, meaning: the seven earths. For this reason it was emphasized by His saying *jamiʿan* (entirely), and ﴿the heavens﴾ was joined to it by conjunction, and it is plural, and the position is one of magnification, so it requires exaggeration. The *qabda* (handful) is the single occurrence of grasping, and with a *ḍamma* (*qubḍa*) it is the amount grasped by the palm. It is said of the amount: *qabḍatuhu* with a *fatha*, as a naming of it by its measure, so this meaning is possible here. It is also possible that the verbal noun is intended with an omitted annexed noun, meaning: possessors of a handful, that is, He grasps them in a single grasp. The earths, despite their vastness and expanse, do not reach beyond the handful of a palm. ﴿Entirely﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial (*hal*).

Al-Hawfi said: The governing element in the circumstantial is what *qabḍatuhu* indicates. End of quotation.

It is not permissible for *qabḍatuhu* to govern it, whether it is a verbal noun or whether the amount is intended.

Al-Zamakhshari said: And with the intention of collectivity, meaning in the earth, and that by it is meant the collective, he said: its emphasis by *al-jamiʿ* (the whole) followed *al-jamiʿ* as an emphasis before the coming of that report, so that it is known at the outset that the report that comes does not refer to one earth, but to all the lands. End of quotation.

He did not mention the governing element of the circumstantial. ﴿On the Day of Resurrection﴾ is an object of *qabḍatuhu*. Al-Hasan read ﴿His handful﴾ with the accusative. Ibn Khalawayh said: by estimating *fi* (in), that is *fi qabḍatihi*; this is the view of the Kufans.

As for the people of Basra, they do not permit that, just as one does not say "Zayd a house." End of quotation.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He made it an adverbial of time, likening the time to an indefinite. Ibn ʿIsa and al-Juʿhadari read ﴿folded up﴾ (*maṭwiyyat*) with the accusative as a circumstantial, and with ﴿and the heavens﴾ conjoined to ﴿the earth﴾, so it is within the scope of ﴿and the earth﴾, and so all is His handful. This reading was used as evidence by al-Akhfash for the permissibility of "Zayd standing in the house," since ﴿and the heavens﴾ is parsed as a subject (*mubtada'*), ﴿by His right hand﴾ as the predicate, and the circumstantial and the prepositional phrase are placed before. There is no proof in it, since ﴿and the heavens﴾ is conjoined to ﴿and the earth﴾ as we have said, ﴿by His right hand﴾ is attached to ﴿folded up﴾, and ﴿folded up﴾ is from *tayy* (folding), which is the opposite of *nashr* (spreading), as He said, Exalted: ﴿On the Day We fold up the heaven like the folding of a scroll for documents﴾ [al-Anbiya': 104], and the custom of one who folds a scroll is to fold it with his right hand. It was also said: His handful is His possession without opponent or rival, and *bi-yamīnihi* means: by His power.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It was also said: ﴿folded up by His right hand﴾ means: annihilated by His oath, because He swore that He would annihilate them. Then he proceeded to deflect those who interpreted it this way with what (p-441) is to be considered in his book. He estimated their greatness only with what was preceded by the mention of its counterpart, since in what came before there was mention of the condition of the earth and the heavens on the Day of Resurrection, so He said: ﴿And the Trumpet will be blown﴾. Is the blowing of the Trumpet three times or two blasts? The view of the majority is that the blast of terror is the blast of swooning, and *al-sa'q* (swooning) here means death, that is: those in the heavens and those on the earth die.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: The *ṣūr* here is the horn, and nothing other than this can be conceived here. As for one who says the *ṣūr* is the plural of *ṣūra* (form), his statement applies only to the blast of resurrection. It is narrated that between the two blasts is forty. End of quotation, and it was not specified.

The reading of Qatada and Zayd ibn ʿAli here is *fi al-ṣuwar* with a *fatha* on the *waw*, the plural of *ṣūra*, which contradicts the view of Ibn ʿAtiyyah, because here it is not conceivable except that it is the horn. Rather, this blowing into the *ṣūr* would be figurative for the approach of death and the departure of the soul.

Qur'anic reading "فَصَعِقَ" with a ḍamma on the ṣād (read as "fa-ṣuʿiqa"). ﴿Then whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth swoons, except whom Allah wills﴾. The apparent meaning of the exception is that ﴿whom Allah wills﴾ are those who ﴿are not struck﴾, i.e. who do not die. Those excepted are: Jibrīl (Gabriel), Mīkā'īl (Michael), Isrāfīl (Seraphiel), and the Angel of Death; or Riḍwān, keeper of Paradise, and the ḥūr (maidens of Paradise), Mālik (keeper of Hell), and the zabāniyya (the guardians of Hell); or the one excepted is Allah Himself. These are the opinions, the last of which is attributed to al-Ḥasan, and the one before it to al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

It is said that the exception refers to those who died before the first blast, i.e. whoever is in the heavens and the earth dies except those whose death has already preceded, because they had already died. This is like the verse ﴿They will not taste death therein, except the first death﴾ [al-Dukhān 44:56]. And ﴿Then it will be blown into again, a second time﴾. The word "ukhrā" (a second time) may be in the accusative position, with the prepositional phrase (al-jār wa-l-majrūr, the prepositional phrase) standing in place of the subject, as was done in the first case. It may also be in the nominative position, serving as the subject, as is explicitly stated in His words: ﴿When the Trumpet is blown with a single blast﴾ [al-Ḥāqqa 69:13].

﴿Then they are standing, looking on﴾, meaning they are alive, their bodies and souls having been restored to them. ("Yanẓurūn", they look on) means they are waiting for what they will be commanded, or waiting to see what will be done to them, or turning their eyes in every direction like the gaze of one stunned when a great calamity has struck him.

The apparent meaning of "qiyām" (standing) is its opposite, sitting, because the mind is seized by them. Zayd ibn ʿAlī read "qiyāman" with the accusative, as a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative, describing the state of the subject). The predicate of the subject (khabar al-mubtadaʾ, the predicate of the nominal subject) is the adverbial phrase (ẓarf, adverbial complement of time or place) which is "idhā" of sudden surprise (idhā al-fujāʾiyya, the "idhā" of sudden occurrence), and this is a necessary ḥāl, since it is the seat of the benefit, unless the predicate is assumed to be omitted, meaning: then they are resurrected, i.e. present, standing.

If you read "qiyāman" as a ḥāl, then the element governing it is that omitted predicate. If we say the predicate is omitted and there is no governing element, then the governing element is the one governing the adverbial phrase. If "idhā" is an adverb of place, as Sībawayh's statement implies, then the estimate is: then in the presence of [them] they are standing. If it is an adverb of time, as al-Riyāshī held, then the estimate is: then at that time in which it was blown, they are, i.e. their existence [is so]. This estimated noun ("their existence") had to be supplied because an adverb of time cannot serve as a predicate about a body. If "idhā" is a particle, as the Kufans claimed, then the predicate must be estimated, unless one holds that "yanẓurūn" is the predicate, and "yanẓurūn" is then the governing element of the ḥāl.

Al-Jumhūr read "wa-ashraqat" in the active voice, meaning it shone. Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr and Abū l-Jawzāʾ read it in the passive voice, from "sharaqat bi-l-ḍawʾ yashruqu" (it was filled with light and saturated with it), and "ashraqahā Allāh" (Allah made it shine), as you say "mala'a al-arḍa ʿadlan wa-ṭabbaqahā ʿadlan" (he filled the earth with justice and covered it with justice). This was stated by al-Zamakhsharī.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: This only applies to a transitive verb. So this would be as if one said: "ashraqa al-bayt" (the house shone) and "ashraqahu al-sirāj" (the lamp made it shine), so the verb is both transitive and intransitive, like "rajaʿa" and "rajaʿtuhu" (he returned and I returned him), and "waqafa" and "waqaftuhu" (he stopped and I stopped him).

The "earth" in this verse is the earth changed from the known earth. The meaning of "ashraqat" is: it shone and its light became great. End of quotation.

The author of al-Lawāmiḥ said: On this reading, "ishrāq" must be transferred from "sharaqat al-shams" (the sun rose) when it rose, so that it becomes transitive by the verb, meaning: it removed the darkness of the earth. It is not permissible for it to be from "ashraqat" meaning it shone, for that is intransitive. This has been made transitive to "the earth" because the agent is not mentioned, and the earth was placed in its position. This is in line with what some later scholars held, without having preceded in it, because some verbs are both transitive and intransitive in one pattern. End of quotation.

In the authentic ḥadīth: "People will be gathered on a white earth, pure as a loaf of clean bread, with no landmark on it for anyone" (p-442) ﴿by the light of its Lord﴾. It is said: Allah creates a light on the Day of Resurrection, and clothes the surface of the earth with it, so the earth shines by it. Ibn ʿAbbās said: The light here is not from the sun and moon, but is a light that Allah creates which illuminates the earth.

It is related that on that day the earth is of silver. The meaning: it shone with a light that Allah Most High created, which He attributed to Himself as an attribution of ownership to the Owner.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: Allah uses the word "light" metaphorically for the Truth, the Qur'an and the proof in several places in the revelation, and this is one of them. The meaning: the earth shone with what He establishes upon it of truth and justice, and the spreading of equity in good deeds, and the weighing of good and evil deeds. This is indicated by the fact that the attribution is metaphorical: it is attributed to His name, because He is the Truth, the Just. The attribution of His name to the earth is because He adorns it when He spreads His justice upon it, sets up the scales of His equity in it, and judges with truth among its inhabitants. You will not see any places more beautiful than justice, nor more prosperous for them than it.

People say to a just king: "The horizons have shone by your justice, and the world has been illuminated by your equity," just as they say: "The lands have been darkened by the tyranny of so-and-so."

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Injustice is darkness on the Day of Resurrection." Just as He opened the verse with the affirmation of justice, He closed it with the negation of injustice.

﴿And the Book will be placed﴾, meaning the scrolls of deeds. It is singular because it is a collective noun (ism jins, a noun of genus denoting a kind), and each person has his own book. Whoever said that "the Book" here means the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawḥ al-Maḥfūẓ) was far off the mark. This is related from Ibn ʿAbbās, but it may not be authentic, and it has been weakened on the ground that the verse is presented in the context of a threat within a report.

﴿And the prophets will be brought﴾ to bear witness against their nations, ﴿and the witnesses﴾. It is said: this is the plural of "shāhid" (witness), and they are those who bear witness to people concerning their deeds.

It is said: they are the messengers among the prophets. It is said: they are the community of Muḥammad (ﷺ), who bear witness for the messengers.

ʿAṭāʾ, Muqātil and Ibn Zayd said: they are the recording angels (al-ḥafaẓa).

Ibn Zayd also said: they are the prophets, the angels, the community of Muḥammad (peace be upon him), and the limbs. Qatāda said: "al-shuhadāʾ" is the plural of "shahīd" (martyr/witness), and there is no threat in it, which is the purpose of the verse.

﴿And judgment will be passed between them﴾ [al-Zumar 39:75], meaning between all creation, and for this reason they are afterwards divided into two groups: the people of the Fire and the people of Paradise, ﴿with truth﴾, meaning with justice.

﴿And every soul will be paid in full﴾, meaning it will be recompensed completely.

﴿And He is most knowing of what they do﴾, so He has no need of a scribe or a witness. In this is a warning and an increase in threat.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 39, verses 64–70 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Say, "Do you order me to worship other than God, you ignorant ones?"﴾ ﴿And it has been revealed to you and to those before you: "If you associate partners with God, your deeds will surely be nullified, and you will surely be among the losers."﴾ ﴿Rather, worship God alone, and be among the thankful.﴾ ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure, while the earth entirely will be His handful on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens will be folded up in His right hand. Glory be to Him, exalted above what they associate with Him.﴾ ﴿And the Trumpet will be blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will swoon, except whom God wills. Then it will be blown again, and behold, they will be standing, looking on.﴾ ﴿And the earth will shine with the light of its Lord, the Book will be placed, the prophets and the witnesses will be brought, and judgment will be passed between them with truth, and they will not be wronged.﴾ ﴿And every soul will be paid in full for what it did, and He is most knowing of what they do.﴾

It is narrated that the polytheists said to the Messenger (peace be upon him): "Touch some of our gods, and we will believe in your God." The word *ghayra* (other than) is in the accusative, governed by *a'budu* (I worship).

Al-Akhfash said: *ta'murunni* is cancelled (*mulgha*, i.e., has no grammatical effect). He also said: *afa-ghayra* is in the accusative governed by *ta'murunni*, not by *a'budu*, because the relative clause (*al-sila*) does not govern what precedes it, since the relative pronoun (*al-mawsul*) has been deleted and the noun has taken the nominative, as in the line of poetry:

"Ah, you who restrain me from entering the battle,"

The relative clause together with the relative pronoun is in the accusative position as a substitute (*badal*) for it. That is: "Do you order me to worship other than God?" Its meaning: "Do you order me to worship other than God?"

Al-Zamakhshari said: Or it is governed by what the sentence *ta'murunni a'budu* implies, because it means: "You worship and say to me, 'I worship it,' and 'Do you say to me that I worship other than God?' Likewise, 'Do you order me to worship other than God?' Do you order me that I worship?" The evidence for the soundness of this view is the reading of those who read *a'buda* with the accusative, meaning with a *fatha* on the *dal*, by implying *an* (that). The majority read *ta'murunni* with the *nun* assimilated into the *nun of protection* (*nun al-wiqaya*), with the *ya'* quiescent. Ibn Kathir read it with a *fatha* on the *ya'*.

Ibn Amir read *ta'murunnani* with two *nun*s, according to the original form. Nafi' read *ta'muruni* with a single *nun* that is kasra-d and a *fatha* on the *ya'*. Ibn Atiyyah said: This is by deleting the single *nun*, which is the one that prepares for the *ya'* of the speaker. The first *nun* may not be deleted; that would be a grammatical error (*lahn*), because it is the sign of the nominative of the verb. End of quotation.

There is disagreement on this matter. Some say the deleted one is the *nun* of nominative case (*nun al-raf'*), and some say it is the *nun* of protection. It is not an error, because the construction is agreed upon, and the disagreement concerns which of the two was deleted. We choose that it is the *nun* of the nominative.

Since the command to worship other than God proceeds only from a foolish ignorant person, He addressed them with the description that requires this, saying: ﴿you ignorant ones﴾.

Since association with God is impossible for one whom God has protected, the phrase ﴿if you associate partners﴾ must be interpreted as addressed to the hearer, and the address continues on this interpretation. What supports this interpretation is that the singular address in ﴿if you associate partners﴾ is not a direct return of the address to the Messenger, for if he were the one addressed, the construction would be *la'in ashraktuma* (if you two associate partners), so that the pronoun would include those before him, and the address would be given precedence.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, "The ones referred to are a group, so how does He say ﴿if you associate partners﴾ in the singular?" I say: its meaning is: "If it is revealed to you, if you associate partners, your deed will be nullified, and to those before you likewise, and it is revealed to you and to each one of them ﴿if you associate partners﴾," as you say, "He clothed us with a garment," meaning each one of us. If you say, "How is this statement valid, given God's knowledge that His messengers do not associate partners and their deeds are not nullified?" I say: it is on the basis of supposition and impossibilities, whose supposition is valid. Then he mentioned words that are to be considered in his book. End of quotation.

This verse is used as evidence that the deeds of an apostate, including prayer and other acts, are nullified. ﴿Was revealed﴾ (*uhiya*) is in the passive voice. It appears that the revelation is these sentences from His words ﴿if you associate partners﴾ up to ﴿among the losers﴾. This is not permissible according to the school of the Basrans, because sentences cannot function as the subject, so they cannot stand in place of the subject.

Muqatil said: It was revealed to you concerning monotheism (*bi-l-tawhid*), and monotheism is omitted. Then he said: ﴿If you associate partners, your deeds will surely be nullified﴾, and the address is to the Prophet (peace be upon him) specifically. End of quotation.

So what stands in place of the subject is the prepositional phrase, which is *ilayka* (to you), and *bi-l-tawhid* is an optional element (*fadla*) whose deletion is permissible because what precedes it indicates it.

The majority read ﴿will surely be nullified﴾ in the active voice, with ﴿your deed﴾ as its subject, in the nominative. It was also read as *layuhbitanna* with a *ya'*, from *ahbata* (to nullify), with *'amalahu* in the accusative, meaning: God will surely nullify your deed, or association will nullify your deed. It was also read with a *nun*, that is *lanuhbitanna 'amalaka* with the accusative, and the divine name is in the accusative governed by ﴿worship﴾ (*fa-'bud*) according to the pattern of their saying: "Zayd, so strike him." It has a full treatment in grammar, and how this *fa'* entered.

Al-Farra' said: If you wish, its accusative can be by a verb hidden before it, as if it were estimated: "Worship God, so worship Him."

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿Rather, worship God alone﴾, as a response to what they ordered him to do of touching some of their gods, as if he said: "Do not worship what they order you to worship. Rather, if you are wise, worship God." So the condition was deleted, and the advancing of the object was made a substitute for it. End of quotation.

The advancing of the object cannot be a substitute for the condition, because it is permissible to say: "Zayd, then Amr, strike," so if it were a substitute, it would not be permissible to combine both.

﴿And be among the thankful﴾, for His blessings, the greatest of which is guidance to the religion of God. ʿIsa read *Bal Allahu* (with *Allahu* in the nominative), while the majority read it in the accusative.

﴿They did not measure God with His true measure﴾, meaning they did not know Him with true knowledge, and they did not estimate Him in themselves with His true estimation, since they associated others with Him and equated Him with stone and wood in worship.

Al-A'mash read ﴿with His true measure﴾ with a *fatha* on the *dal*. Al-Hasan, ʿIsa, Abu Nawfal and Abu Haywah read ﴿they did not measure﴾ with a shadda on the *dal*, and ﴿with His true measure﴾ with a *fatha* on the *dal*, meaning: they did not truly magnify Him. The pronoun in ﴿they measured﴾ — Ibn ʿAbbas said: it refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh. This whole verse was a discourse addressed to them and a refutation of them. It was also said that it was revealed concerning a group of Jews who spoke about the attributes of God and His majesty, so they denied and anthropomorphized Him and brought every kind of confusion. This sentence is mentioned in al-Anʿam, in al-Hajj, and here.

When He informed them that they had not known Him with true knowledge, He alerted them to His greatness and the sublimity of His station, by way of depiction and imagination, saying: ﴿while the earth entirely will be His handful on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens will be folded up in His right hand﴾.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The purpose of this statement, when taken as it is in its whole and collectively, is to depict His greatness and to bring attention to the reality of His majesty only, without taking the handful or the right hand toward a literal direction or a figurative direction. End of quotation.

He means: "or a specific figurative direction." The informing is depiction, and imagination is from figurative language. Others said: The basic principle in speech is to take it on its literal meaning. If a separate proof establishes the impossibility of taking it literally, then it must be turned to figurative meaning.

So the words "handful" and "right hand" are literal in reference to the organ, but the rational proof stands on the impossibility of attributing organs and limbs to God the Exalted. Therefore it is necessary to take it as figurative. That is because one says: "So-and-so is in the handful of so-and-so," when he is under his management and control, and from it comes ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾ [al-Muʾminun: 6], where the meaning is that it is owned by them. "This house is in the hand of so-and-so," and "so-and-so took such-and-such and it came into his handful," meaning his sole possession of it. All of this is widespread figurative usage in common use.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: Here the right hand and the handful are an expression for power, and whatever comes to mind in the breast other than this is false.

What al-Qadi (meaning Ibn al-Tayyib) held, that they are attributes additional to the essential attributes, is a weak view, and according to what comes to mind in souls which knowledge has not encompassed.

He said, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Glory be to Him, exalted above what they associate with Him﴾, meaning: He is free from all the doubts that do not befit Him. End of quotation.

Al-Qaffal said: This is like the saying of one who says: "He did not estimate me with my true estimation, and I am the one who did such-and-such," meaning: since you know that my condition and attribute are this which I have mentioned, it is necessary that you not err concerning my rank and station. Its parallel is: ﴿How can you disbelieve in God when you were dead and He gave you life?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 28], meaning: how can you disbelieve in One whose attribute and dominion are this? So likewise here: ﴿they did not measure God with His true measure﴾, meaning: they claimed that He has partners, and that He cannot give life to the dead, though the earth and the heavens are in the handful of His power. End of quotation.

﴿And the earth﴾, meaning: the seven earths. For this reason it was emphasized by His saying *jamiʿan* (entirely), and ﴿the heavens﴾ was joined to it by conjunction, and it is plural, and the position is one of magnification, so it requires exaggeration. The *qabda* (handful) is the single occurrence of grasping, and with a *ḍamma* (*qubḍa*) it is the amount grasped by the palm. It is said of the amount: *qabḍatuhu* with a *fatha*, as a naming of it by its measure, so this meaning is possible here. It is also possible that the verbal noun is intended with an omitted annexed noun, meaning: possessors of a handful, that is, He grasps them in a single grasp. The earths, despite their vastness and expanse, do not reach beyond the handful of a palm. ﴿Entirely﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial (*hal*).

Al-Hawfi said: The governing element in the circumstantial is what *qabḍatuhu* indicates. End of quotation.

It is not permissible for *qabḍatuhu* to govern it, whether it is a verbal noun or whether the amount is intended.

Al-Zamakhshari said: And with the intention of collectivity, meaning in the earth, and that by it is meant the collective, he said: its emphasis by *al-jamiʿ* (the whole) followed *al-jamiʿ* as an emphasis before the coming of that report, so that it is known at the outset that the report that comes does not refer to one earth, but to all the lands. End of quotation.

He did not mention the governing element of the circumstantial. ﴿On the Day of Resurrection﴾ is an object of *qabḍatuhu*. Al-Hasan read ﴿His handful﴾ with the accusative. Ibn Khalawayh said: by estimating *fi* (in), that is *fi qabḍatihi*; this is the view of the Kufans.

As for the people of Basra, they do not permit that, just as one does not say "Zayd a house." End of quotation.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He made it an adverbial of time, likening the time to an indefinite. Ibn ʿIsa and al-Juʿhadari read ﴿folded up﴾ (*maṭwiyyat*) with the accusative as a circumstantial, and with ﴿and the heavens﴾ conjoined to ﴿the earth﴾, so it is within the scope of ﴿and the earth﴾, and so all is His handful. This reading was used as evidence by al-Akhfash for the permissibility of "Zayd standing in the house," since ﴿and the heavens﴾ is parsed as a subject (*mubtada'*), ﴿by His right hand﴾ as the predicate, and the circumstantial and the prepositional phrase are placed before. There is no proof in it, since ﴿and the heavens﴾ is conjoined to ﴿and the earth﴾ as we have said, ﴿by His right hand﴾ is attached to ﴿folded up﴾, and ﴿folded up﴾ is from *tayy* (folding), which is the opposite of *nashr* (spreading), as He said, Exalted: ﴿On the Day We fold up the heaven like the folding of a scroll for documents﴾ [al-Anbiya': 104], and the custom of one who folds a scroll is to fold it with his right hand. It was also said: His handful is His possession without opponent or rival, and *bi-yamīnihi* means: by His power.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It was also said: ﴿folded up by His right hand﴾ means: annihilated by His oath, because He swore that He would annihilate them. Then he proceeded to deflect those who interpreted it this way with what (p-441) is to be considered in his book. He estimated their greatness only with what was preceded by the mention of its counterpart, since in what came before there was mention of the condition of the earth and the heavens on the Day of Resurrection, so He said: ﴿And the Trumpet will be blown﴾. Is the blowing of the Trumpet three times or two blasts? The view of the majority is that the blast of terror is the blast of swooning, and *al-sa'q* (swooning) here means death, that is: those in the heavens and those on the earth die.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: The *ṣūr* here is the horn, and nothing other than this can be conceived here. As for one who says the *ṣūr* is the plural of *ṣūra* (form), his statement applies only to the blast of resurrection. It is narrated that between the two blasts is forty. End of quotation, and it was not specified.

The reading of Qatada and Zayd ibn ʿAli here is *fi al-ṣuwar* with a *fatha* on the *waw*, the plural of *ṣūra*, which contradicts the view of Ibn ʿAtiyyah, because here it is not conceivable except that it is the horn. Rather, this blowing into the *ṣūr* would be figurative for the approach of death and the departure of the soul.

Qur'anic reading "فَصَعِقَ" with a ḍamma on the ṣād (read as "fa-ṣuʿiqa"). ﴿Then whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth swoons, except whom Allah wills﴾. The apparent meaning of the exception is that ﴿whom Allah wills﴾ are those who ﴿are not struck﴾, i.e. who do not die. Those excepted are: Jibrīl (Gabriel), Mīkā'īl (Michael), Isrāfīl (Seraphiel), and the Angel of Death; or Riḍwān, keeper of Paradise, and the ḥūr (maidens of Paradise), Mālik (keeper of Hell), and the zabāniyya (the guardians of Hell); or the one excepted is Allah Himself. These are the opinions, the last of which is attributed to al-Ḥasan, and the one before it to al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

It is said that the exception refers to those who died before the first blast, i.e. whoever is in the heavens and the earth dies except those whose death has already preceded, because they had already died. This is like the verse ﴿They will not taste death therein, except the first death﴾ [al-Dukhān 44:56]. And ﴿Then it will be blown into again, a second time﴾. The word "ukhrā" (a second time) may be in the accusative position, with the prepositional phrase (al-jār wa-l-majrūr, the prepositional phrase) standing in place of the subject, as was done in the first case. It may also be in the nominative position, serving as the subject, as is explicitly stated in His words: ﴿When the Trumpet is blown with a single blast﴾ [al-Ḥāqqa 69:13].

﴿Then they are standing, looking on﴾, meaning they are alive, their bodies and souls having been restored to them. ("Yanẓurūn", they look on) means they are waiting for what they will be commanded, or waiting to see what will be done to them, or turning their eyes in every direction like the gaze of one stunned when a great calamity has struck him.

The apparent meaning of "qiyām" (standing) is its opposite, sitting, because the mind is seized by them. Zayd ibn ʿAlī read "qiyāman" with the accusative, as a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative, describing the state of the subject). The predicate of the subject (khabar al-mubtadaʾ, the predicate of the nominal subject) is the adverbial phrase (ẓarf, adverbial complement of time or place) which is "idhā" of sudden surprise (idhā al-fujāʾiyya, the "idhā" of sudden occurrence), and this is a necessary ḥāl, since it is the seat of the benefit, unless the predicate is assumed to be omitted, meaning: then they are resurrected, i.e. present, standing.

If you read "qiyāman" as a ḥāl, then the element governing it is that omitted predicate. If we say the predicate is omitted and there is no governing element, then the governing element is the one governing the adverbial phrase. If "idhā" is an adverb of place, as Sībawayh's statement implies, then the estimate is: then in the presence of [them] they are standing. If it is an adverb of time, as al-Riyāshī held, then the estimate is: then at that time in which it was blown, they are, i.e. their existence [is so]. This estimated noun ("their existence") had to be supplied because an adverb of time cannot serve as a predicate about a body. If "idhā" is a particle, as the Kufans claimed, then the predicate must be estimated, unless one holds that "yanẓurūn" is the predicate, and "yanẓurūn" is then the governing element of the ḥāl.

Al-Jumhūr read "wa-ashraqat" in the active voice, meaning it shone. Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr and Abū l-Jawzāʾ read it in the passive voice, from "sharaqat bi-l-ḍawʾ yashruqu" (it was filled with light and saturated with it), and "ashraqahā Allāh" (Allah made it shine), as you say "mala'a al-arḍa ʿadlan wa-ṭabbaqahā ʿadlan" (he filled the earth with justice and covered it with justice). This was stated by al-Zamakhsharī.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: This only applies to a transitive verb. So this would be as if one said: "ashraqa al-bayt" (the house shone) and "ashraqahu al-sirāj" (the lamp made it shine), so the verb is both transitive and intransitive, like "rajaʿa" and "rajaʿtuhu" (he returned and I returned him), and "waqafa" and "waqaftuhu" (he stopped and I stopped him).

The "earth" in this verse is the earth changed from the known earth. The meaning of "ashraqat" is: it shone and its light became great. End of quotation.

The author of al-Lawāmiḥ said: On this reading, "ishrāq" must be transferred from "sharaqat al-shams" (the sun rose) when it rose, so that it becomes transitive by the verb, meaning: it removed the darkness of the earth. It is not permissible for it to be from "ashraqat" meaning it shone, for that is intransitive. This has been made transitive to "the earth" because the agent is not mentioned, and the earth was placed in its position. This is in line with what some later scholars held, without having preceded in it, because some verbs are both transitive and intransitive in one pattern. End of quotation.

In the authentic ḥadīth: "People will be gathered on a white earth, pure as a loaf of clean bread, with no landmark on it for anyone" (p-442) ﴿by the light of its Lord﴾. It is said: Allah creates a light on the Day of Resurrection, and clothes the surface of the earth with it, so the earth shines by it. Ibn ʿAbbās said: The light here is not from the sun and moon, but is a light that Allah creates which illuminates the earth.

It is related that on that day the earth is of silver. The meaning: it shone with a light that Allah Most High created, which He attributed to Himself as an attribution of ownership to the Owner.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: Allah uses the word "light" metaphorically for the Truth, the Qur'an and the proof in several places in the revelation, and this is one of them. The meaning: the earth shone with what He establishes upon it of truth and justice, and the spreading of equity in good deeds, and the weighing of good and evil deeds. This is indicated by the fact that the attribution is metaphorical: it is attributed to His name, because He is the Truth, the Just. The attribution of His name to the earth is because He adorns it when He spreads His justice upon it, sets up the scales of His equity in it, and judges with truth among its inhabitants. You will not see any places more beautiful than justice, nor more prosperous for them than it.

People say to a just king: "The horizons have shone by your justice, and the world has been illuminated by your equity," just as they say: "The lands have been darkened by the tyranny of so-and-so."

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Injustice is darkness on the Day of Resurrection." Just as He opened the verse with the affirmation of justice, He closed it with the negation of injustice.

﴿And the Book will be placed﴾, meaning the scrolls of deeds. It is singular because it is a collective noun (ism jins, a noun of genus denoting a kind), and each person has his own book. Whoever said that "the Book" here means the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawḥ al-Maḥfūẓ) was far off the mark. This is related from Ibn ʿAbbās, but it may not be authentic, and it has been weakened on the ground that the verse is presented in the context of a threat within a report.

﴿And the prophets will be brought﴾ to bear witness against their nations, ﴿and the witnesses﴾. It is said: this is the plural of "shāhid" (witness), and they are those who bear witness to people concerning their deeds.

It is said: they are the messengers among the prophets. It is said: they are the community of Muḥammad (ﷺ), who bear witness for the messengers.

ʿAṭāʾ, Muqātil and Ibn Zayd said: they are the recording angels (al-ḥafaẓa).

Ibn Zayd also said: they are the prophets, the angels, the community of Muḥammad (peace be upon him), and the limbs. Qatāda said: "al-shuhadāʾ" is the plural of "shahīd" (martyr/witness), and there is no threat in it, which is the purpose of the verse.

﴿And judgment will be passed between them﴾ [al-Zumar 39:75], meaning between all creation, and for this reason they are afterwards divided into two groups: the people of the Fire and the people of Paradise, ﴿with truth﴾, meaning with justice.

﴿And every soul will be paid in full﴾, meaning it will be recompensed completely.

﴿And He is most knowing of what they do﴾, so He has no need of a scribe or a witness. In this is a warning and an increase in threat.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 39, verses 64–70 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Say, "Do you order me to worship other than God, you ignorant ones?"﴾ ﴿And it has been revealed to you and to those before you: "If you associate partners with God, your deeds will surely be nullified, and you will surely be among the losers."﴾ ﴿Rather, worship God alone, and be among the thankful.﴾ ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure, while the earth entirely will be His handful on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens will be folded up in His right hand. Glory be to Him, exalted above what they associate with Him.﴾ ﴿And the Trumpet will be blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will swoon, except whom God wills. Then it will be blown again, and behold, they will be standing, looking on.﴾ ﴿And the earth will shine with the light of its Lord, the Book will be placed, the prophets and the witnesses will be brought, and judgment will be passed between them with truth, and they will not be wronged.﴾ ﴿And every soul will be paid in full for what it did, and He is most knowing of what they do.﴾

It is narrated that the polytheists said to the Messenger (peace be upon him): "Touch some of our gods, and we will believe in your God." The word *ghayra* (other than) is in the accusative, governed by *a'budu* (I worship).

Al-Akhfash said: *ta'murunni* is cancelled (*mulgha*, i.e., has no grammatical effect). He also said: *afa-ghayra* is in the accusative governed by *ta'murunni*, not by *a'budu*, because the relative clause (*al-sila*) does not govern what precedes it, since the relative pronoun (*al-mawsul*) has been deleted and the noun has taken the nominative, as in the line of poetry:

"Ah, you who restrain me from entering the battle,"

The relative clause together with the relative pronoun is in the accusative position as a substitute (*badal*) for it. That is: "Do you order me to worship other than God?" Its meaning: "Do you order me to worship other than God?"

Al-Zamakhshari said: Or it is governed by what the sentence *ta'murunni a'budu* implies, because it means: "You worship and say to me, 'I worship it,' and 'Do you say to me that I worship other than God?' Likewise, 'Do you order me to worship other than God?' Do you order me that I worship?" The evidence for the soundness of this view is the reading of those who read *a'buda* with the accusative, meaning with a *fatha* on the *dal*, by implying *an* (that). The majority read *ta'murunni* with the *nun* assimilated into the *nun of protection* (*nun al-wiqaya*), with the *ya'* quiescent. Ibn Kathir read it with a *fatha* on the *ya'*.

Ibn Amir read *ta'murunnani* with two *nun*s, according to the original form. Nafi' read *ta'muruni* with a single *nun* that is kasra-d and a *fatha* on the *ya'*. Ibn Atiyyah said: This is by deleting the single *nun*, which is the one that prepares for the *ya'* of the speaker. The first *nun* may not be deleted; that would be a grammatical error (*lahn*), because it is the sign of the nominative of the verb. End of quotation.

There is disagreement on this matter. Some say the deleted one is the *nun* of nominative case (*nun al-raf'*), and some say it is the *nun* of protection. It is not an error, because the construction is agreed upon, and the disagreement concerns which of the two was deleted. We choose that it is the *nun* of the nominative.

Since the command to worship other than God proceeds only from a foolish ignorant person, He addressed them with the description that requires this, saying: ﴿you ignorant ones﴾.

Since association with God is impossible for one whom God has protected, the phrase ﴿if you associate partners﴾ must be interpreted as addressed to the hearer, and the address continues on this interpretation. What supports this interpretation is that the singular address in ﴿if you associate partners﴾ is not a direct return of the address to the Messenger, for if he were the one addressed, the construction would be *la'in ashraktuma* (if you two associate partners), so that the pronoun would include those before him, and the address would be given precedence.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, "The ones referred to are a group, so how does He say ﴿if you associate partners﴾ in the singular?" I say: its meaning is: "If it is revealed to you, if you associate partners, your deed will be nullified, and to those before you likewise, and it is revealed to you and to each one of them ﴿if you associate partners﴾," as you say, "He clothed us with a garment," meaning each one of us. If you say, "How is this statement valid, given God's knowledge that His messengers do not associate partners and their deeds are not nullified?" I say: it is on the basis of supposition and impossibilities, whose supposition is valid. Then he mentioned words that are to be considered in his book. End of quotation.

This verse is used as evidence that the deeds of an apostate, including prayer and other acts, are nullified. ﴿Was revealed﴾ (*uhiya*) is in the passive voice. It appears that the revelation is these sentences from His words ﴿if you associate partners﴾ up to ﴿among the losers﴾. This is not permissible according to the school of the Basrans, because sentences cannot function as the subject, so they cannot stand in place of the subject.

Muqatil said: It was revealed to you concerning monotheism (*bi-l-tawhid*), and monotheism is omitted. Then he said: ﴿If you associate partners, your deeds will surely be nullified﴾, and the address is to the Prophet (peace be upon him) specifically. End of quotation.
